author: Comunizar
title: Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria
content:
¿Qué está pasando?


            En las últimas semanas hemos visto una serie de eventos que parecen abrir la esperanza de un cambio en la dirección de las luchas sociales. Estamos pensando en primer lugar en las protestas en las calles de Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países. También hemos visto la derrota de la derecha en una serie de elecciones: Hungría, Serbia, Brasil, Estados Unidos. Pero al mismo tiempo y, sobre todo, sigue el genocidio en Gaza. ¿Qué está pasando?


            ¿Cómo entender la serie de protestas de las últimas semanas en Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países? ¿Hasta qué punto se está abriendo, sobre todo entre lxs jóvenes, una perspectiva o una forma de organización que va contra-y-más-allá del capitalismo? ¿Es la rabia -volcánica- la conexión entre todas esas luchas actuales y pasadas?


            ¿Cómo entender la derrota de la derecha en las elecciones? ¿Pensamos que hay una diferencia significativa entre un gobierno de extrema derecha y uno de centro-izquierda? ¿Pensamos que el descontento expresado en esas elecciones podría desbordar la forma-Estado?


            ¿Cómo entender las luchas actuales en el marco del genocidio en Gaza? ¿En la virulencia de las recientes protestas en varios países de Europa, no estará escondido también un grito de impotencia/desahogo por el genocidio impune de Gaza? ¿Hay una rabia que esté tratando de salir del encierro que este sistema genocida nos impone? ¿Es posible sostener la esperanza crítica de un mundo otro no capitalista en un mundo que no ha logrado impedir ni detener el genocidio en Gaza?


Call for Papers


What’s Going On?


           

 In recent weeks we’ve seen a series of events that seem to open hope for a change in the direction of social struggle. We are thinking in the first place of the protests in the streets of France, Italy, Portugal, Germany, Albania, India and many other countries. And we have also seen the defeat of the right in a series of elections: Hungary, Serbia, Brazil, the Unites States. But at the same time, and above all, the genocide continues in Gaza. What’s going on?


            How do we understand the protests in all these countries? To what extent can we see, especially amongst the young, a perspective that goes against-and-beyond capitalism? To what extent are these protests breaking with the state-form and creating communising or other forms of organisation? Is volcanic rage the connection between all these struggles of the present and the past?


            How do we understand the defeat of the right in the various elections? Do we think that there is a significant difference between a government of the extreme right and one of the centre-left? Do we think that the discontent expressed in these elections could overflow from the state-form?


            How do we understand these struggles in the context of the genocide in Gaza? Does the virulence of these protests reflect a scream of hopelessness or fury in the face of the unpunished genocide in Gaza? In the violence of these protests is there a rage that is trying to break the enclosure that this genocidal system imposes on us? Is it still possible to maintain the hope of a world beyond capitalism in a world that has not succeeded in stopping the genocide in Gaza? In this context, of what significance are the elections in the USA or the visit of the Pope to Argentina and other countries of South America?


The post

Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria

 first appeared on

Comunizar

.

author: By Camilla Conzelli, Contributor
title: Trans Teacher Fired, Then Held in Men’s Cell, as Turkey Escalates Crackdown on LGBTQIA+ People
content:
Istanbul, Turkey — Months after being fired, trans teacher Zoe Lila was detained at a Sept. 15 protest against the “My Family Is Safe” operation, Turkey’s crackdown on LGBTQIA+ people, and she was held in a men’s cell.


“I was a queer kid, I’ve been discriminated against since childhood, and I never felt included in the school system,” Zoe Lila said. “That’s why teaching isn’t just a job for me: it means being there as an educator, making sure no human being experiences any kind of discrimination.”


Lila is a young Turkish trans woman who has worked in education for 10 years. In 2021, she started teaching English at a private school, Açı Middle School in Istanbul. “It’s an international school that welcomes many minorities and bases its approach on human rights,” she explained. “So I felt like I had finally found my place.”


Zoe Lila


In 2024, when she began hormone replacement therapy, Lila told the school’s administration about her transition. “Their first reaction was, ‘It’s your right, we’ll support you,’” she recalled. Encouraged by that support, she decided to stay in Turkey, despite a long and complex process.


Reyda Ergün, an academic working on LGBTQIA+ rights, said the country is one of the worst examples of a medicalized model for gender affirmation.


Under the

current legal framework

, vaginoplasty or phalloplasty is a binding prerequisite for legal recognition. The surgery can only be authorized by a court, and the person must have a diagnosis of “transsexualism” certifying that surgery is necessary for their mental health. After the operation, a second court proceeding begins in which a judge has the discretion to decide whether the procedure was “sufficient and appropriate” to change the person’s biological characteristics.


Since 2018, Ergün has co-authored an annual report published by

Kaos GL

, an organization that monitors the employment conditions of LGBTQIA+ people in Turkey’s

public

 and

private

 sectors.


Over the years, the data has revealed that

concealing one’s identity

 is the primary means of self-defense workers adopt for fear of retaliation or dismissal.


In this context, trans people are especially vulnerable. “The long and complex nature of the affirmation and legal recognition process can expose people to further discrimination and job insecurity,” Ergün said. “When changes in official records and physical appearance become visible before legal recognition has been obtained, concealment strategies are no longer viable, and the risks that had been averted until then materialize.”


Zoe Lila’s story is a textbook example. In the summer of 2026, she completed the process leading to her gender-affirming surgery. In mid-June, she first came out to her colleagues and then, during a dedicated session led by a psychologist, to her 120 students. The reaction at school was initially warm and welcoming, but a few days later, everything fell apart.


A parent sent Lila’s photo and personal information to pro-government media, setting off a virulent hate campaign. Newspapers published her image with a cross over her face, revealing all of her personal data and the details of the school where she worked.


“It was horrible. It was the most unfair, unethical and unlawful article I’ve ever read in my life. And the person it was talking about was me,” Lila said. Soon she began receiving death threats and insults, including from her own family. Feeling unsafe, she left her apartment and moved in with a friend.


Meanwhile, Turkey’s Ministry of National Education intervened directly at the school. Under threat of sanctions and mass layoffs, school administrators caved to the political pressure. On June 24, 2026, just 10 hours before her long-scheduled vaginoplasty, the school told Lila it would not renew her contract.


“I was fired 10 hours before the surgery, and it was devastating,” she said. The operation went ahead as planned, but Lila suddenly found herself without a job, without income and at the center of a violent attack. She immediately turned to a lawyer to take legal action, but ran up against Turkish labor law: private school teachers are typically hired on renewable one-year contracts, which rules out a lawsuit for reinstatement.


Still, the fight continues through complaints filed with the relevant authorities and the creation of a

solidarity network

. “We don’t want financial compensation,” Lila said. “We want this to be an act of defense for trans and LGBTQ+ …

title: (KIEL, GER) Revolutionäre Frauensponti zum 25.11.
content:
Wir haben uns heute als Frauen und alle die als solche unterdrückt werden, kämpferisch die Straße und die Nacht genommen!


Jede von uns kennt die Angst davor alleine im Dunkeln nach Hause zu laufen, die Angst davor verfolgt und belästigt zu werden. Jede von uns kennt patriarchale Gewalt. Doch wir haben von klein auf gelernt zu akzeptieren, was uns angetan wird. Gelernt darüber zu schweigen und die Schuld bei uns selbst zu suchen. Aber diese Gewalt ist Teil des patriarchalen und kapitalistischen Systems und sie ist dafür da uns einzuschüchtern und unten zu halten.


Wir sagen: Es reicht!


Um diesem System den Kampf anzusagen, müssen wir uns zusammenschließen, lernen gemeinsam zu kämpfen und uns auferlegte Rollenbilder zu durchbrechen. So wird Angst in Stärke und Mut verwandelt und wir verstehen, dass wir uns diese zu nutzen machen können.


Auch müssen gerade wir als Frauen eine militante Haltung und daraus hervorgehend, eine militante Praxis entwickeln. Denn unsere Befreiung wird nicht mit Worten erkämpft werden. Dabei können wir lernen, von den Kämpferinnen der YPG, von der feministischen Bewegung Lateinamerikas und so vielen weiteren Genossinnen aus der ganzen Welt. Denn wir werden uns nur selbst schützen. Und nur wir können dem Ursprung der patriarchalen Gewalt, diesem kapitalistischen und patriarchalem System etwas entgegensetzen. Kämpfen wir also gemeinsam für den revolutionären Bruch und den Aufbau des Kommunismus!


Für die Feministische Revolution!


Heraus zum Tag gegen Gewalt an Frauen!


Anmerkung des Moderationskollektiv von barrikade.info: «Unsere Sprache spiegelt gesellschaftliche Machtverhältninsse und Unterdrückungsformen wieder. Dazu gehören Sexismus und die erzwungene Geschlechterbinarität. Dies äussert sich u.a. in der Nutzung einer binären Sprache. Dies bedeutet, dass nur in den Kategorien «Frau» und «Mann» gedacht und geschrieben wird. Als Kollektiv einer emanzipatorischen, anti-autoritären Medien-Plattform erwarten wir eine diskrimiierungsfreie Haltung. Die Geschlechtsbinarität stellt eine Unterdrückung dar und die Verwendung binärer Sprache in Momenten, in denen die Schreibenden die Geschlechtsidentität der Menschen nicht kennen und/oder Identitäten, welche nicht in dieser Binarität Platz haben, unsichtbar gemacht werden, ist diskriminierend.


Anstelle von binären Begriffen kann in solchen Momenten genderneutrale Sprache verwendet werden (z.B. Demonstrierende). Auch kann versucht werden, durch andere Begriffe die gewünschte Menschengruppe zu beschreiben (z.B. TINFA*), sowie kann auf die Nutzung von Genderzeichen, wie dem Genderstern, zurückgegriffen werden. Oder durch die Nennung, wer nicht gemeint ist, lassen sich ebenfalls inklusive Menschengruppen schaffen (z.B. alle, welche nicht Teil der hegemonialen Männlichkeit sind).


Natürlich gibt es noch weitere Möglichkeiten, welche genutzt werden können.

author: Holly Jonas
title: How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want
content:
This article

How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Kumi Naidoo knows a thing or two about activism. He has organized anti-apartheid school boycotts in South Africa, scaled oil rigs in frigid Arctic waters and called out world leaders for their moral failures in U.N. climate negotiations. But it was not until he eulogized a glacier that he truly realized the potent alchemy of arts, culture and activism — also known as artivism.


With decades of experience in social movements and serving in top leadership positions in international NGOs, Naidoo is better placed than most to shed light on the inner workings of activism. He is also refreshingly candid about its shortcomings. One of the biggest challenges in activism, he says, is a communications deficit. His late son, South African rapper and singer Riky Rick, lovingly pushed him to ditch the technical jargon so commonly used by climate activists and instead reach people through the heart, body and soul.


After the musician’s devastating and sudden passing in 2022, Riky’s mother Louisa, widow Bianca, and Kumi channeled their grief and resolve into the Riky Rick Foundation for the Promotion of Artivism. One of their key initiatives,

Global Artivism

, highlights the power of arts and culture to contribute to positive change, helps cultural creatives connect and collaborate with each other, and surfaces and works to address the many challenges they face. Powered by a team of volunteers and a lean staff, in-person global convenings in South Africa and Brazil and regional virtual convenings have helped mobilize and further energize this vibrant movement. They are now in the thick of the decentralized

Global Artivism Month

, which will culminate on International Human Rights Day on Dec. 10.


In this interview with Naidoo, who also serves as president of the

Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative

, he discusses the power and potential of the global artivism movement, how pessimism is a luxury we cannot afford, and the continuing prescience of Martin Luther King Jr.


This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.


For those who may not be familiar with it, what is artivism, and what are the connections between artivism and nonviolent movements?


Artivism is the intersection of arts, culture and activism. Its intention is to address a major weakness in much of our activism, which is that we have aimed our messages and our narratives at the brain, and we’ve ignored the heart, the body and the soul. A song or documentary reaches many more people than a policy brief does. Politics does not drive culture; culture drives politics.


Harnessing the power of arts and culture on its own will not deliver salvation from the climate crisis and the intersecting crises that emerge from it. However, failing to harness the power of arts and culture almost guarantees that we’re going to fail because we’re never going to reach the large numbers of people that we need to.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


We are facing a massive global mental health crisis coming from ecological and climate anxiety, war, conflict, deepening inequality, authoritarianism and fascism. Artivism has the potential to invite people into the biggest struggles of our time, in a way that creates opportunities for participation and engagement. To help us secure peace, justice and all of the good things that we want, those in power have no incentive to actually listen to what we’re saying unless we can show we have a powerful constituency.


We also need this massive mobilization and participation because participation itself will be part of the antidote to despair, despondency and depression. We can be the best versions of ourselves in this current moment if we keep a positive disposition, despite how bad things are. In this moment of history, pessimism is a luxury we simply cannot afford. The pessimism that justifiably emerges from our analysis, our lived experiences and observations can and must be responded to with the optimism of our thought, our action, our creativity, our courage and our sense of humanity.


Joyful acts of cultural expression, in which hope is embedded, offer us the best way forward. Artivism is typically nonviolent, creative and speaks to the heart. I believe artivism has a big role in the quest to create a world where we value peace and we value nonviolence …

author: David Swanson
title: “Disaster Waiting to Happen”: Iowa Declares Emergency as U.S. Army Detonates 5 Tons of Lead Azide
content:
By Democracy Now, November 25, 2026


The U.S. Army detonated nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, potentially sending toxic lead dust and other deadly contaminants spewing across communities and farmland throughout the Mississippi River water basin. Residents, who were first informed last week, had been ordered to evacuate or else shelter in place. “The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts,” says Pat Elder, who tracks how military activity impacts people and the planet at the Military Poisons project. “There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen.” 


Pat Elder is a member of the Board of World BEYOND War.

author: Sam Bright
title: Farage Relaunches Brexit Campaign Alongside Pro-Truss Economist
content:
Reform UK

 leader

Nigel Farage

 has relaunched his Leave.EU pro-Brexit campaign alongside a prominent ally of former Prime Minister

Liz Truss

.


Catherine McBride addressed the Keep Britain Out event alongside Farage and major Brexit funder Arron Banks as they ramp up their opposition to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s attempts to forge a closer relationship with the EU.


McBride, who has held positions at right-wing pro-Brexit groups for a number of years, has vocally defended Truss and her disastrous ‘mini budget’ of September 2022.


Farage has been keen to distance himself from the former prime minister’s record despite suggestions that the pair overlap on economic policy. The Reform leader

called

 the mini budget, which announced £45 billion in unfunded tax cuts and government spending, “the best Conservative budget since 1986”.


However, with Farage attempting to prove his economic credentials, he has since changed his tune on Truss – saying that she

wouldn’t be welcome

 in his party.


That sits uncomfortably with Farage’s alliance with McBride – who has continued to cheerlead for Truss.


McBride and Farage had a similar response to the mini budget. On 1 October 2022, a week after its release, McBride

wrote an article

 for Briefings for Britain that enthusiastically endorsed the economic package, stating: “Three cheers for Liz Truss and her Chancellor”.


Just 19 days later, with the

pound plummeting

 and

borrowing costs surging

, Truss announced her resignation as prime minister.


However, unlike Farage, McBride has not backed away from Truss. In July 2023, she wrote an article for The Critic – a magazine funded by Reform donor

Jeremy Hosking

 – entitled “

Why Truss was right

”. In the piece, McBride claimed it’s an urban myth that Truss wrecked the economy, saying “the evidence doesn’t support it.”


During the Keep Britain Out event, Farage said the campaign was “incredibly fortunate” to have McBride involved.

But McBride has also been happy to share a platform with Truss,

interviewed on her podcast

 in February 2026 during which the pair claimed that a “socialist green lobby” is the real threat to the UK economy.


McBride is also a vocal advocate of increased fossil fuel extraction in the UK and has questioned basic climate science.


Appearing before the House of Commons International Trade Committee in March 2023,

she said

: “I do not see carbon dioxide as this great poison” – adding that she is “very cynical” about the climate emergency.


In reality, climate impacts are already being seen in the UK and across the world, with 5,200

heat-linked deaths

 in England this summer – almost double the previous high of 2,900 in 2022. Amid a succession of heatwaves, England also suffered its

worst harvest on record

, with three-quarters of Brits now concerned about climate change, according

to polling

 by Ipsos.


However, McBride supports policies that would ramp up UK fossil fuel output and contravene our climate commitments. In

an interview

 with the Institute of Economic Affairs – a libertarian pressure group

historically funded

 by oil majors – McBride called for the windfall tax on oil companies to be lifted, the ban on new exploration licences to be scrapped, and a reversal of the UK’s net zero commitments.


McBride has also called for the prohibition on fracking for shale gas to be lifted – a stance championed by Truss –

saying

 that we shouldn’t ban the practice simply because it would “spoil the view” in the “north of England”.


In reality, fracking is banned in the UK due to its 

environmental and health impacts

.


McBride shares her climate opposition with Farage, who has

claimed

 it’s “nuts” for CO2 to be considered a pollutant. Reform supports the mass expansion of fossil fuel production in the UK, including of coal, and the scrapping of clean energy schemes.


That is despite the rising price of fossil fuels

largely being responsible

 for the increased household energy prices suffered since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the

world’s leading climate scientists warning

 that human-caused emissions are driving extreme weather events, including droughts, flooding, and wildfires.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Huna": Egyptian Author Abdelrahman ElGendy on Prison, National Book Award & Being Denied U.S. Visa
content:
This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut,

Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming

, chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an

MFA

 in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.


“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells

Democracy Now!

 about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”


We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet

Mada Masr

, whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.


“

Mada

 carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in

Mada Masr

. “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

title: Ephéméride des luttes : 26 novembre
content:
Humeur combative pour ce 26 novembre de l'éphéméride des luttes, aux quatre coins du globe. Il faut dire qu'on est bien déterminé-e-s à ne pas se laisser faire.


1920 :

 En Ukraine, les bolcheviks rompent leur seconde alliance avec Makhno, et l'armée rouge attaque Goulai-Polé, siège de la Maknovtchina, mais Makhno réussira à s'enfuir.


1927 :

 A Buenos Aires, l'anarchiste Italien Severino Di Giovanni fait sauter l'usine de cigarettes Combinados. Celle-ci avait lancé une nouvelle cigarette « pour ouvriers » qu'elle avait nommée la « Sacco et Vanzetti » (trois jours plus tôt, les deux anarchistes de Boston avaient été exécutés sur la chais électrique) afin de plaire tout de suite et d'économiser des frais d'électricité.


1970 :

 La Nouvelle Résistance Populaire (liée à la Gauche Prolétarienne) enlève le député Michel De Grailly, instigateur de nombreuses lois répressives et idéologue de la Cour de Sûreté de l'État.


1972 :

 A Dublin, probablement l'IRA fait sauter une bombe à l'extérieur du cinéma Film Centre vers 1h30 du matin.


1977 :

 A Paris, manifestation contre l'expulsion des squats du 14e arrondissement : 1000


personnes dont 300 autonomes : un squat expulsé est démuré, le siège de la SEMIREP et un car de police sont incendiés.


1978 :

 A Belfast, Albert Miles, responsable de la prison de Crumlin Road, est abattu devant chez lui par l'IRA.


1981 :

 A Garac (Gers), le Mouvement d'action révolutionnaire antinucléaire (MARAN) fait sauter un relais hertzien des PTT.


1983 :

 A Toulouse, le CLODO (Comité Liquidant et Détournant les Ordinateurs), composé de 'travailleurs de l'informatique', incendie les locaux de Speery Univac Ordinateur.


1984 :

 A Bierset, près de Liège, les Cellules Communistes Combattantes (CCC) font sauter deux pylônes et leurs installations au sol d'un centre de télécommunications de la base aérienne, qui accueille les chasseurs-bombardiers de l'OTAN.


2010 :

 A Rio de Janeiro, plus de 21.000 policiers surarmés investissent plusieurs favelas de la ville dans le but de les "pacifier", accompagnés de véhicules blindés et de soldats. Au moins 49 personnes sont tuées par balles au cours des plusieurs jours que dure cette "opération".


2013 :

 A Tegucigalpa, capitale hondurienne, des affrontements violents éclatent dans le cadre d'une lutte étudiante contre des résultats électoraux falsifiés.


2014 :

 Au Chili, dans la province de Talagante près de Santiago, le 'Groupe Anarchiste Coordonné (GAC) - Bande Organisée Mauricio Morales / Cellule Incendiaire Sebastián Oversluij' bloque des voies ferrées avec de gros rochers et des pneus incendiés en solidarité avec les anarchistes Tamara Sol Farías et Sebastián Oversluij.


2015 :

 A Tlanepantla dans la province de Puebla au Mexique, une manifestation a lieu contre le maire et sa politique. Rapidement, la manifestation tourne à l'affrontement contre la police venue réprimer la grogne, des molotovs font leur apparition et plusieurs véhicules du maire sont incendiés.


 A Maracaibo au Venezuela, c'est un bus qui est brûlé par un groupe de manifestant-e-s masqué-e-s lors d'une protestation.


2019 :

author: Unknown
title: Ahmet Saymadi neden hâlâ tutuklu?
content:
Ahmet Saymadi, 5 Ekim 2026’dan bu yana tutuklu. Hakkındaki suçlama, Türk Ceza Kanunu’nun 190. maddesinde düzenlenen “uyuşturucu veya uyarıcı madde kullanılmasını kolaylaştırma” suçu. Ancak aradan geçen zamana, yapılan aramalara ve toplanan delillere rağmen kamuoyunun önüne bu suçlamayı somutlaştıran tek bir olgu konulmuş değil.


Ortada delil olmadığı için bu soru orta yerde durmaya devam ediyor: O zaman Ahmet Saymadi neden hâlâ tutuklu?


3 Ekim gecesi, saat 23.00 sıralarında, Ahmet Saymadi’nin sahibi olduğu Kadim Meyhanesi polisler tarafından basıldı. Bir ihbar gerekçe gösterilerek gerçekleştirilen baskında işletmede bulunan 89 müşterinin kimlik kontrolleri ve üst aramaları yapıldı. İşletme kapsamlı biçimde arandı. Ancak yapılan aramalarda herhangi bir uyuşturucu maddeye veya suç unsuruna rastlanmadı.


Ne işletmede ne Ahmet Saymadi’nin üzerinde ne de çalışanlarında uyuşturucu madde bulunduğuna ilişkin bir bulgu ortaya konuldu. Müşteriler üzerinde yapılan kontrollerde de suçlamayı destekleyecek bir sonuç açıklanmadı.


Buna rağmen Ahmet Saymadi gözaltına alındı ve 5 Ekim’de tutuklandı.


Savcılık ifadesinde kendisine yöneltilen ilk soru uyuşturucu kullanıp kullanmadığıydı. Ahmet, hayatı boyunca uyuşturucu kullanmadığını, sigara dahi içmediğini söyledi. Ardından soruşturmanın odağı değişti. Türkiye İşçi Partisi Milletvekili ve gazeteci Ahmet Şık’ı tanıyıp tanımadığı, aralarında ticari bir ilişki bulunup bulunmadığı ve banka hesapları arasındaki bazı para hareketleri soruldu.


Ahmet, uzun yıllardır dostu olan Ahmet Şık’ın kredi kartıyla işletmesi için bazı alışverişler yaptığını, hesaplar arasındaki para transferlerinin de bu harcamaların karşılığı olduğunu anlattı. Bu açıklamaları destekleyen banka kayıtları avukatları tarafından dosyaya sunuldu.


Peki, bütün bunların uyuşturucu kullanılmasını kolaylaştırma suçlamasıyla nasıl bir bağlantısı var? Ahmet Saymadi’nin kime, ne zaman, nerede ve hangi davranışıyla uyuşturucu kullanımını kolaylaştırdığına ilişkin somut delil nerede?


Bu soruların yanıtı hâlâ kamuoyuna açıklanmış değil.


Tutukluluk, fiilî cezaya dönüşüyor


Ceza yargılamasında tutuklama bir ceza değildir. Henüz suçluluğu kesinleşmemiş bir insanın özgürlüğünün sınırlandırılması ancak kanunun öngördüğü koşullarda ve zorunlu hâllerde başvurulabilecek istisnai bir tedbirdir.


Anayasa’nın 19. maddesi kişi özgürlüğü ve güvenliği hakkını güvence altına alır. Ceza Muhakemesi Kanunu’nun 100. maddesi ise tutuklama için kuvvetli suç şüphesini gösteren somut delillerin ve bir tutuklama nedeninin bulunmasını şart koşar.


Ahmet Saymadi dosyasında ise işletme aranmış, müşteriler kontrol edilmiş, gerekli incelemeler yapılmış ve soruşturmanın konusu olan olası deliller toplanmıştır. Avukatları, bu koşulları ve dosyadaki eksiklikleri göstererek iki kez tutukluluğun gözden geçirilmesi için başvuruda bulundu. Ancak bu başvurulardan sonuç alınamadı. Şimdi yeni bir dilekçe daha savcılığın önünde bekliyor.


Eğer deliller toplanmışsa, aramalar tamamlanmışsa ve karartılabilecek bir delil durumu kalmamışsa tutukluluğun devamını gerektiren neden nedir?


Üstelik Ahmet, bu süreçte Metris Cezaevi’nden Silivri Cezaevi’ne sevk edildi ve uyuşturucu dosyalarından tutuklu bulunan kişilerin kaldığı 50 kişilik bir koğuşa yerleştirildi. Bir insanın özgürlüğünden yoksun bırakılması yetmiyormuş gibi, tutukluluk koşullarının da ayrıca ağırlaşması kabul edilebilir mi?


Ahmet’in tutukluluğu neredeyse iki ayı bulmuş durumda. Bu süre uzadıkça, henüz yargılama sonunda hüküm verilmeden tutuklama fiilî bir cezalandırmaya dönüşmüş oluyor zaten. Polis baskını ve basına yansıyan haberlerin ardından işletmenin zaten ciddi biçimde zorlandığı da biliniyor. Ahmet’in işinin başına dönmesinin, yaşamını sürdürebilmesinin ve savunmasını özgürce hazırlayabilmesinin önünde neden hâlâ engel bulunuyor?


Ahmet Şık ve Yonca Şık hakkındaki iddialar


Ahmet Saymadi’nin tutuklanmasıyla ilgili süreçte kamuoyuna çeşitli iddialar da yansıdı. TİP Milletvekili Ahmet Şık, X hesabından yaptığı bir açıklamada, bir paylaşımını silmemesi hâlinde Ahmet Saymadi’nin tutuklanacağı yönünde kendisine haberler ulaştığını aktarmıştı.


Ardından Ahmet Şık’ın eşi Yonca Şık da “casusluk” iddiasıyla gözaltına alındı. Yonca Şık tutuklanmadı; ancak hakkında yurt dışına çıkış yasağı şeklinde adli kontrol tedbiri uygulandı.


Bu gelişmelerin Ahmet Saymadi’nin tutuklanmasıyla nasıl bir ilişkisi olduğu, soruşturma süreçlerinin hangi bağlantılar üzerinden yürütüldüğü elbette ortaya …

title: “Να τσακίσουμε την σκευωρία Marfin”: Δράση στην πορεία για την Εξέγερση του Πολυτεχνείου (Βίντεο)
content:
“Να τσακίσουμε την σκευωρία Marfin”: Δράση στην πορεία για την Εξέγερση του Πολυτεχνείου (Βίντεο)


Βίντεο

 από τη δράση αλληλεγγύης και αντιπληροφόρησης ενάντια στη σκευωρία Marfin Vol. 3 στην πορεία μνήμης για την Εξέγερση του Πολυτεχνείου στις 17 Νοέμβρη 2026.


Λίγα λόγια για την υπόθεση της Marfin, μέσα από αποσπάσματα της εφημερίδας δρόμου

Άπατρις:


“Η ανακίνηση της υπόθεσης Marfin για 3η φορά σηματοδοτεί το πέρασμα σε μια νέα εποχή όσον αφορά τον εγχώριο κοινωνικό-ταξικό ανταγωνισμό.


Στις 10 Ιουλίου εκτελείται τριπλό ένταλμα σύλληψης, και διατάσσονται κατ’ οίκον έρευνες σε 5 άτομα. Συλλαμβάνονται οι σύντροφοι Θύμιος και Κώστας, και η συντρόφισσα Ελένη, κάτοικος εξωτερικού, που μεταφέρεται στα αγγλικά κρατητήρια.


Τα στοιχεία για την υπόθεση είναι ανύπαρκτα: Από την έκθεση της Διεύθυνσης Εγκληματολογικών Ερευνών, όπου αναλύεται το οπτικοακουστικό υλικό, δεν προκύπτει ταυτοποίηση των συντροφιών ως παρόντα στο σημείο μπροστά από την τράπεζα. Μοναδικά στοιχεία η ομοιότητα κάποιων κινητών αντικειμένων, και ένα ανώνυμο email, το οποίο συνέταξε η Διεύθυνση Αντιμετώπισης Οργανωμένου Εγκλήματος που πραγματοποίησε τις συλλήψεις. Η δουλειά της αστυνομίας είναι πολύ πρόχειρη: Στο mail αναφέρεται ως μέλος στο «παρεάκι» που εμπλέκεται στην υπόθεση, άτομο που ήταν στη φυλακή εκείνη την ημέρα· ακόμα, η εκπρόσωπος τύπου της ΕΛ.ΑΣ., Κ. Δημογλίδου, αναφέρει στον ΣΚΑΪ πως το επίμαχο mail είναι στα χέρια της αστυνομίας 1,5 χρόνο, ενώ αυτό έχει ημερομηνία αποστολής 08/04/2026, δηλαδή 3 μήνες πριν τις συλλήψεις.


Οι απολογίες διεξάγονται ενώπιον της ανακρίτριας Σμαράγδας Τασούλη, και της εισαγγελέως Βαρβάρας Γνεσούλη. Τα συντρόφια αρνούνται τις κατηγορίες, υπερασπίζονται την πολιτική τους θέση, όπως και τη συμμετοχή τους στη διαδήλωση, και ζητούν να διερευνηθεί ποιος έστειλε το e-mail.


Και τα 3 συντρόφια προφυλακίζονται παρά την απουσία στοιχείων. Απορρίπτονται και οι προσφυγές τους ενάντια στην απόφαση προφυλάκισης, καθώς τα αρμόδια Συμβούλια πλημμελειοδικών επικυρώνουν τις απορριπτικές προτάσεις των εισαγγελέων, του αντιεισαγγελέα πρωτοδικών Λυμπερόπουλου, και των εισαγγελέων πρωτοδικών Μαρουδά και Ηλιοπούλου. Έχει ενδιαφέρον πως στα σκεπτικά των προφυλακίσεων, όπως και στις απορρίψεις των προσφυγών, υιοθετείται η συλλογιστική από το διαβιβαστικό της αστυνομίας, εμπλουτισμένη με αναφορές σε «ενδείξεις ενοχής» αλλά και σε «οργανωμένη, συλλογική και προπαρασκευασμένη δράση». Σύμφωνα με τους δικαστικούς, υπάρχει ο κίνδυνος τα συντρόφια μας να τελέσουν τα ίδια αδικήματα, μιας και «εδώ και 16 χρόνια κρύβουν επιμελώς τη δράση τους». Τι πιο λογικό άλλωστε;


Η ΔΑΟΕ, κατ’ εντολή του Μιχάλη Χρυσοχοΐδη, έκανε τη δουλειά της. Στο μαγείρεμα παίρνει θέση και η δικαστική εξουσία, έτοιμη να το αναβαθμίσει με την –όχι και τόσο– μυστική συνταγή της. Η υπόθεση μένει στην εποπτεία της ανακρίτριας Τασούλη για τις τελικές πινελιές και το ντεκόρ.


Οι νέες συνταγές, λοιπόν, δεν αργούν. Το μαγειρείο καλά κρατεί: Στις αρχές Οκτώβρη, η ανακρίτρια επιστρατεύει την 1η παράγραφο του νόμου 187Α, αυτήν περί ατομικής τρομοκρατίας.* Μέχρι πρότινος τα 3 συντρόφια κατηγορούνταν για ανθρωποκτονία κατά συρροή και από κοινού, και τα διαθέσιμα «στοιχεία» δεν επαρκούσαν για τη απόδοση κατηγοριών σύστασης οργάνωσης (εγκληματικής ή τρομοκρατικής). Με αυτή τη μεθόδευση, το κατηγορητήριο αναβαθμίζεται. Αυτό επιφέρει επιπλέον κατηγορίες για 24 απόπειρες ανθρωποκτονίας – κατηγορίες που δεν παραγράφονται εφόσον η πράξη υπάγεται στην αντιτρομοκρατική νομοθεσία.


Το σημαντικότερο όλων, όμως, όταν έρθει η ώρα της δίκης, είναι πως τα συντρόφια μας δεν θα οδηγηθούν σε ΜΟΔ, όπως συνέβη με την πρώτη εκδίκαση της υπόθεσης (για ακριβώς τα ίδια αδικήματα, εξαιρουμένου του 187Α). Αντιθέτως, θα δικαστούν από Τριμελές Εφετείο Κακουργημάτων, που θα απαρτίζεται μόνο από επαγγελματίες δικαστές. Έτσι, αφήνεται εκτός ο αστάθμητος παράγων των ενόρκων, που έχουν οδηγήσει σε πανηγυρικές αθωώσεις αγωνιστών ανά τα χρόνια – όπως εξάλλου συνέβη και στην πρώτη version της υπόθεσης, με το ίδιο ακριβώς κατηγορητήριο.


Συνολικά από την πλευρά του κράτους, η ανακίνηση της υπόθεσης Marfin έρχεται ως κλείσιμο ενός ανοιχτού λογαριασμού, που βαστάει τουλάχιστον 2 δεκαετίες – λογαριασμός που άνοιξε με τη μαζικοποίηση των κοινωνικών αντιστάσεων, και την κορύφωσή της κατά την τριετία των αντιμνημονιακών ταραχών (2010-2012). Ο κατασταλτικός μηχανισμός δεν ενδιαφέρεται πραγματικά να βρει τους «ενόχους του τότε», αλλά να τρομοκρατήσει τους «συνενόχους του σήμερα» – όσες και όσους δεν έχουν πλέον πολλές …

author: Memuna Konteh
title: The mountains we miss
content:
Ahmed Koroma’s

Freetown Echoes: Tales from Along the Odokoko

 traces a city in the process of transformation through the eyes of a boy becoming. The novel is a collection of stories, sitting somewhere between fiction, folklore and memoir, in which a young Ahmed and his friends are shaped by their community, like rocks in the stream that flows through it. The cadence and colorful cast of characters in the stories are distinctly Sierra Leonean, while the tension, optimism and anticipation dripping through the pages will be familiar to anyone, African or otherwise, who knows the necessary unease of surrendering to an environment with energy greater than the sum of its inhabitants.

The novel paints a portrait of Freetown in its prime: lush green hills towering over a bubbling metropolis, where market-women, morimen and ministers mingle under the hot sun, everyone hustling for their daily bread. Along the Odokoko, a decade on from independence, things progress and pause to the pulse of a youthful, overzealous nation, where the prospect of perpetually “developing” has not yet been corrupted into the geopolitical hallmark of damnation that it is today. As someone born toward the tail of Sierra Leone’s civil war, Ahmed’s Freetown is not a Freetown that I recognize. It is, however, a Freetown I can embrace with open arms, and respect immensely, like one would the grandparent of a close friend.

The Freetown I know is rebellious and resigned in equal measure. Its hills still loom majestically over a bright and busy coastline, but much of the greenery has been replaced, razed in favor of concrete compounds. The city is in a constant state of construction, never quite finished. The hustlers, in the many forms they take, grow in number by the day, always hungry, too consumed by the never-ending grind to stop and acknowledge each other properly. By night, my Freetown becomes a playground much like the riverbank where Ahmed and his friends would run riot. It’s a place where I can party, free of all inhibition, from dusk until daybreak.

The resulting atmosphere is a chaos that enchants me on my frequent visits from the UK. From a perspective hued by privilege, I see Freetown as a boot camp for my patience, one I enter willingly. I can look upon the frequent blackouts, traffic bottlenecks, broken-down buildings on beach road, overpriced entertainment complexes and overcrowded malls, cramped club dancefloors and palm-body slums with affection or righteous indignation. I’ve no use for the armor of apathy worn by full-time Freetonians with no alternative home.

In Ahmed’s Freetown — one he looks back on from comforts hard-won in California — the Cotton Tree still stands tall; Victoria Park is lush with greenery and the Sierra Leone Library is a free and accessible sanctuary for bookworms across the city. More than just fuel for nostalgia, memorializing Freetown’s history in this way allows us to imagine (and thus enact) better for Freetown’s future. But this book is not a call to arms. It makes no judgments about the country’s politics and presents no arguments as to where things went wrong. It is reflective, retrospective and seductive in its simplicity, leaning on age-old traditions of Sierra Leonean storytelling. Because it’s written from a personal place, concerned more with capturing emotional truths of the protagonist’s childhood than anything else, it avoids the traps of preachiness and didacticism that African historical fiction sometimes falls victim to.

Silky prose and dynamic dialogue usher the reader through a series of tragedies and triumphs, weaving in wives’ tales and local legends for cultural grounding. The country’s layered spiritual tapestry comes to the fore in stories like Aladura, Eku Mason and The Girl Who Has Eyes; in When Death Came, and A Child is Born, we see both grief and glory held collectively as sacrament; and in The Days of Elephant, Baby Moon, and Bad Kahina we see how the rhythms of a community can be shifted by a handful of imposing individuals. Each story provides its own window into different aspects of the Sierra Leonean psyche. We meet dancers, chiefs, teachers, thieves, nurses, herbalists, pastors, psychics, among many others, all through the equalizing lens of boyhood.

I think much of the novel’s charm can be attributed to that spirit of youth which Ahmed captures so well. It’s a spirit that leads with curiosity, unafraid to call things into question and test its theories, and not yet too …

author: Francesco Rota
title: Moyale and the Limits of Kenya’s Silence on Ethiopia
content:
At the end of October, staff from UNHCR and the Kenya Red Cross began

issuing coded wristbands

 to Ethiopian families sheltering in schools and churches in Moyale, a town in Kenya’s Marsabit County that shares its name, and in practice its streets, with the Ethiopian town across the border. By 29 October around

50,000 people

 had crossed in little more than a week, most of them women and children, and the Kenyan government and its humanitarian partners are now

planning for as many as 80,000

.


These people are not fleeing the war in northern Ethiopia, where fighting resumed in Tigray in late September and federal troops

retook Mekelle on 3 October

. That conflict has also brought Ethiopia and Eritrea to the edge of open war, as the two governments have

broken off diplomatic relations

 and accused each other at the United Nations of

starting a war

. They are fleeing a separate conflict more than a thousand kilometres further south, between two of Ethiopia’s own regional governments. Nevertheless, the two crises are connected, and the connection matters for Kenya, because a war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would make the present numbers at Moyale look small.


A dispute inside Ethiopia, on Kenya’s border


Ethiopian Moyale is shared between the Oromia and Somali regions, which run the town jointly and have argued for decades over the land around it. In the middle of October, Somali regional officials

opened a new office in a district that Oromia claims and raised their regional flag over it

, and a girl of thirteen was

killed in the violence that followed

. Within a few days the security forces of the two regions were fighting each other with heavy weapons inside the town, and the violence

spread to the districts of Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero

.


Clashes along this same boundary in 2017

displaced hundreds of thousands of people

, which suggests that the problem lies in the way Ethiopia’s federal system works rather than in a single provocation. The system gives territory to regions defined by ethnic identity and leaves mixed towns such as Moyale to argue over where they belong. What has changed since 2017 is that the federal army is now heavily committed in the north, and the regional forces in the south have been left to settle the question among themselves. In this sense the two crises meet, since every unit that Addis Ababa sends towards Tigray and the Eritrean border is a unit no longer available to keep rival regional forces apart elsewhere in the country.


Because the border at Moyale runs through the middle of a single town and through communities that live on both sides of it, the fighting has not stayed in Ethiopia. Kenyan police reported

stray bullets

 landing on the Kenyan side within the first week, Kenya Defence Forces teams have since

found and destroyed several grenades

, and a woman in Kenyan Moyale has been

killed by what appears to have been a stray bullet

. Kenya’s acting Commissioner for Refugee Affairs, Mercy Mwasaru, now describes the situation as

a matter of national security

.


Kenya’s selective role in the region


Kenya is sometimes described as a passive observer of conflict in the Horn of Africa, but its record suggests a country that intervenes where it judges its interests to be at stake and stays quiet elsewhere. It sent troops into Somalia in 2011 and still has soldiers there, it hosted the talks that led to the

2005 agreement

 ending the war between northern and southern Sudan, and in November 2022 it hosted the meeting of Tigrayan and federal commanders that produced the

Nairobi Declaration

. Under President William Ruto, Kenya went further on Sudan than any other neighbour by hosting the Rapid Support Forces as they launched a charter for a rival government, a decision that led the military authorities in Sudan to

ban Kenyan imports

.


On Ethiopia, by contrast, Kenya has chosen to say very little, and the reasons for that choice are practical. Ethiopia is Kenya’s largest neighbour and a central economic and security partner. The two governments

revived their 2012 Special Status Agreement

 in 2024, signed a defence cooperation agreement the following year, and in March this year

agreed to carry out joint military operations

 along the road corridor that links Moyale, Marsabit and Turkana. Nairobi has generally treated disorder inside Ethiopia as Ethiopia’s own affair and has handled its effects on Kenyan soil as a humanitarian question …

author: Dauti Kahura
title: How Ruto Lost Gikuyus and What Happens Next?
content:
We recently buried our aunt, Wahito. She hailed from Ndumberi in Kiambu County and was my mother’s elder sister. A staunch Catholic, she was practically buried by the Catholic Women Association. Resplendent in their headscarves and their blue and white uniforms, the CWA practically took charge during the long funeral mass. The officiating priest eulogized my aunt, who died at 87, as a beacon of steadfastness in her Catholicism and reminded us that dead men and women tell no tales. She was gone, and we the living had the duty to reclaim our stories. As he wound up his sermon, the priest asked the congregation whether it was steadfast in its resolve to do the right thing come 10 August 2027. The congregation responded in unison, and the

Wantam

 slogan rent the air. A flash of satisfaction crossed the priest’s face; his smile was unmistakable. At the burial site, the priest was unrelenting: “Once again I implore you, we must do the right thing, and we mustn’t forget.”


The Wantam gospel


The Catholic Church of Kenya, through the powerful voice of Archbishop Anthony Muheria, the Opus Dei cleric overseeing the Nyeri diocese, recently warned its clergy against allowing politics at pulpits across the country. The priest presiding over my aunt’s funeral must have heard Archbishop Muheria loud and clear, but in the Mt Kenya region, the mainstream churches have taken it upon themselves to preach the

Wantam

 gospel, the clarion call that sums up the opposition to President William Ruto, nine months to the general election. The Church was at the forefront of canvassing for votes for Ruto in the Mt Kenya region in the run-up to the 2022 elections, but less than two years later, after the region had overwhelmingly voted for the president, cracks began to appear, and things were falling apart. 


Christian president


Whatever happened? Why has a community that had overwhelmingly voted for Ruto despite all the iniquities that it accused him of having perpetrated against it now with the same vigour, turned its back on him? In a region that is supremely religious, the mainstream churches – the Anglican Church of Kenya (ACK), the Catholic Church, the Methodist Church, and the Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) – play a central role in shepherding their congregations in the direction in which it is going to vote. In the lead-up to the August 2022 elections, the churches threw their support behind Ruto and asked their faithful to follow suit. They cast Ruto as a born-again, bible-reading Christian, as opposed to Raila Odinga, whose Christianity was considered dodgy as far as the Mt Kenya region’s religious leaders were concerned. The clerics looked forward to enhanced social engagements with the forthcoming “Christian president”. But woe unto them, because as they would soon find out, President Ruto’s only interest was to capture state power, after which he would discard their “anointed and holy” support.


Betrayal


That betrayal – the feeling of having been used and abused despite the supposedly gentleman’s agreement on an anticipated state – church revival – is what led the Mt Kenya region’s ACK leadership, barely two years into President Ruto’s rule, to ask their congregations for forgiveness for having campaigned for him and for asking them to do the same and vote for him. As an ACK Mt Kenya diocese elder told me, the Church was truly remorseful for having misled its worshippers and regretted its liaison with a president who had deliberately lied to the Church leadership. Always circumspect in its dealings with the state, the leadership of the powerful Catholic Church of Kenya, through the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB), finds President Ruto insincere in his politics – a euphemism for liar. “He lies like a sieve,” one Catholic priest told me. “He believes that the Catholic Church leadership in Mt Kenya is ‘biased’ against him because he’s not a Catholic. The region’s Catholic clergy didn’t fight Mwai Kibaki; why? Because he was a Catholic. The same clergy didn’t fight Uhuru Kenyatta; why? For the same reason; he is Catholic.” Ruto is caught up in his lies and deceptions, and he has come to believe in those lies, said the priest.   


“Ruto lied to us”


If the Church in the Mt Kenya region has experienced betrayal from Ruto, it is the voter who has verbalized that betrayal. As early as 2024, the Mt Kenya region voter complained about the “punitive taxes” that were introduced, especially on the Hass …

author: WoMin
title: Practising solidarity economy: Women’s collective action and community finance in Memirlosho
content:
Conversations about economic development often portray rural women as people who need support, training, or assistance. Far less attention is paid to how women organise themselves to solve problems, manage resources, and build livelihoods together. During a recent visit to the

Memirlosho Women Cultural Village

 in Isiolo County, northern Kenya, we saw how Samburu women offer a powerful example of a community and solidarity economy in practice. The cultural village brings together four women’s groups (Narasha, Muruguti, Narupa, and Rapunye) that work as a collective to create opportunities, strengthen resilience, and improve livelihoods. Their lived experience demonstrates that solidarity economies are not solely theoretical concepts or future possibilities. They are already being built every day through cooperation, mutual support, and shared responsibility.


Collective organising as a condition for economic agency


The first foundation of Memirlosho’s economic model is collective organising. The women registered a Community Based Organisation (CBO) through which they transformed dispersed individual survival strategies into a legally recognised collective entity. This shift carries important economic and political implications as they gained greater visibility, legitimacy, and bargaining power. The umbrella structure allows the four groups to support one another while maintaining their own identities. Together, they can access external support, coordinate activities, and speak with a stronger collective voice.


More importantly, the organisation creates a sense of shared purpose. Members are no longer facing challenges alone, they have built a community that pools resources, shares risks, and works toward common goals.


Productive activities: turning livelihoods into collective assets


Memirlosho’s economic activities are rooted in skills and resources that already exist within the community. Hence, two productive activities form the backbone of the village. The first is beadwork. Women use their cultural knowledge and craftsmanship to produce traditional beadwork that can be sold for income. Working collectively allows them to purchase materials more efficiently, share information, and explore markets together.


Another important activity is goat rearing and trading. Through support from the

Samburu Women Trust

, the groups received forty goats, with ten goats allocated to each group. Rather than viewing these animals as a one-time gift, the women transformed them into a revolving community asset.


The goats are raised and later sold, with the proceeds used to purchase new livestock. In this way, the original investment continues to generate benefits over time. Instead of being consumed, the asset grows and supports future opportunities. This approach reflects one of the central principles of solidarity economies: resources are managed not only for individual gain but for the long-term benefit of the collective.


Financial solidarity: A savings system built around people’s needs


While productive activities constitute the foundation of

Memirlosho’s

 solidarity economy, the Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) serves as its circulatory system. The VSLA operates as a community-owned financial institution managed according to principles of mutual support rather than external profit extraction. The system has three main characteristics:


a

) Socially oriented lending:

  Women can access loans for socially important needs especially school fees, respond to emergencies, or meet household needs. Interest collected on loans is not extracted by an outside institution. Instead, it returns to the group’s common fund, benefiting all members. This way, capital serves the community’s wellbeing and social reproduction rather than simply financial accumulation.


b) Inclusive flexibility:

 The savings model is also flexible. Members contribute according to their means and circumstances, recognising that income can fluctuate throughout the year, as a pastoral community. This allows participation even during difficult periods and helps ensure that nobody is excluded because they cannot meet rigid contribution requirements. It’s a system that prioritises participation and inclusion.


c) Community control over finance:

 The VSLA enables members to maintain ownership and control over their financial resources. By keeping financial decision-making within the community, the group reduces dependence on …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Two men sentenced for Khayelitsha church sexual assault
content:
On Easter Sunday in 2023, two young men stormed the Showers of Blessings Christian Church in Zion, in Site C carrying a gun and a knife and robbed the women congregants before sexually assaulting and raping them. Yamkela Jobo and Okuhle Beya were found guilty on all 21 charges and were sentenced to 25 years in prison by the regional court in Khayelitsha today.


Thembinkosi Fati, the secretary of South African Zionist Churches, said they welcome the sentencing of the two. “The guilty verdict was a victory on its own, given how cases like this one just disappear into thin air. It might not be exactly what we wanted, but it shows that the investigating officers and the state did a good job,” he said.


According to Fati, Jobo and Beya took advantage of loadshedding, and the fact that the women and children were alone in the church hall where they were sleeping.


Nolukholo Jezile, one of the church leaders, said that they would sleep at the church during Easter. “It’s clear that they planned the attacks on us, because they waited until all the men were gone and they stormed the church,” she said.


She commended the courage of the women of the church for overcoming their trauma. “It was not easy at all; we could have easily given up,” but they are still not able to go to church alone.


Community-based organisations supported the church during the trial, including

Amadoda Aqotho

 and Sidima Sam Gentlemen’s Organisation.


Amadoda Aqotho supported the church members during the trial.


The prosecutors told the court that the pair ordered the congregants to strip naked, robbed 19 women of their cellphones, and sexually assaulted two of them before fleeing.


One of the mitigating circumstances offered by the defence lawyer was that the two young men were abandoned by their parents.


“Not having a parent does not give an excuse to be a thief and a rapist. Instead, it should teach you to be independent. I was not aware that they were this young. The women that the accused assaulted are old enough to be their mothers and grandparents,” said Sabelo Zekevu, the chairperson of Amadoda Aqotho. He called on men to stop abuse and report cases of gender-based violence when they witness them.

author: Abahlali_3
title: South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity
content:
South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity

Address at a public meeting hosted by Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa at the Ellen Melville Centre in Auckland on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Comrades, thank you for inviting me to return to Aotearoa. I bring you greetings of solidarity from Abahlali baseMjondolo, the shack dwellers’ movement of South Africa, which was formed in Durban in 2005 and now has more than 200 000 members across South Africa.

It is fifteen years since I was last here, in 2011, when we commemorated the thirtieth anniversary of the great protests against the Springbok rugby tour of 1981. I want to begin by remembering that history, and by thanking all the people of this country who stood with us against apartheid. People marched, confronted the police, and sometimes faced arrest and violence. You refused to allow the apartheid state to present itself as a normal member of the international community.

This was an outstanding example of international solidarity, and an example that we should seek to emulate in our solidarity with the people of Palestine.

In our movement we speak of living solidarity. This means solidarity that exists in action, not just in words. It means solidarity between people who recognise one another as equals.

Settler colonialism in South Africa and Israel

South Africa and Palestine are both countries that have been oppressed by settler colonialism. This is part of the reason for the long solidarity with Palestine among South Africans.

But there are important differences between these two forms of settler colonialism. In South Africa, the colonial system was organised around the dispossession of Africans from their land, the theft of their cattle and the exploitation of their labour. The economy depended on African workers in the mines, on the farms, in the factories and in the homes of white people. The settlers wanted the land, but they also wanted the labour of the people they had dispossessed.

Huge numbers of people were forced from their homes and land as African people were pushed into ‘reserves’, based on the system used to oppress Native Americans, and later into the ‘Bantustans’, the so-called ‘homelands’. The Bantustans were not just used to confine the African people on tiny bits of land. They were also central to the migrant labour system that ensured cheap labour for white capital and for white families in their homes.

African workers were forced by economic necessity to leave their families and communities to find work in the mines and cities. Many were compelled to live in single-sex hostels, separated from their families. Africans were wanted as workers but rejected as citizens with equal rights. They were systematically dehumanised. This system was maintained through the police, the army, prisons, torture and killing. Those who resisted were treated as criminals and terrorists.

When we look at Palestine today, we recognise many of these methods of oppression. We see a fundamentally racist settler colonial system in which there is ongoing dispossession of people from their land by the Israeli state and settlers. We see homes being demolished. We see communities separated from one another by walls, checkpoints and military restrictions. We see people who stand up against oppression being called ‘terrorists’ and subject to mass imprisonment, torture and murder.

The struggles against racism and for land are central to the struggle for freedom, both in South Africa and in Palestine. But there are also differences between apartheid in South Africa and oppression in Palestine.

While Palestinians have been exploited as workers, the fundamental drive of settler colonialism in Israel is to remove or destroy the Palestinian people rather than to exploit them for their labour.

In South Africa, the apartheid system required the continued presence of a large and hyper-exploited African workforce, while seeking to control, segregate and impoverish it. In Palestine, the settler-colonial project has involved the destruction of Palestinian communities, the removal of Palestinians from their land and the attempt to establish and maintain territorial and political control through their displacement.

The Nakba of 1948 forced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes. Many became refugees in other countries, and they and their descendants remain unable to return. The occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem since 1967 has brought …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Thirty Years On, Intersex Africans Set Their Own Agenda for Rights and Belonging
content:
It was a rare energy, fueled by our shared trials nd triumphs, and by stories that stretched beyond these walls. We, intersex activists from across Africa, came together, gathering on the shoulders of those who paved the way, held together by a promise that our voices would carry us far. Seeing the adoption of the Nairobi Declaration reminded me that our voices are now influencing regional conversations, policies and demands for justice.


We have come a long way. Years ago, people would laugh at you for raising intersex issues in Ghana; today, journalists call us to make documentaries.


On 26 October, we marked thirty years of Intersex Awareness Day. The day commemorates a

1996 protest

 by intersex activists against unnecessary, irreversible surgeries on intersex children and their demand that we decide what happens to our own bodies. Thirty years on, that is still our demand: that we decide. Many gains since then have been won on this continent. South Africa’s equality law has recognised intersex status since 2005. Kenya became the first African country to

count intersex people in a census

 in 2019, and its

Children Act 2022

 recognised intersex children in law. In 2023, the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights adopted

Resolution 552

, calling on states to end non-consensual surgeries, infanticide and abandonment. This year, Zimbabwe’s Minister of Justice

convened a high-level meeting

 on legal recognition, and South Africa’s Human Rights Commission now

guides parents towards alternatives to invasive procedures

.


We are also building  and expanding our spaces.


From 30 September to 2 October, intersex Africans gathered in Nairobi for the first-ever Africa Intersex Movement conference. Activists came from East, Southern, North and West Afric

a.

For the first time, intersex activists, community members, scholars, cultural workers, and allies from across Africa came together.

We told our stories in our own words and s

et our own agenda and demands. It was a community in communion and a platform to press for rights, protection and dignity.


We left with the Nairobi Declaration, whose ten demands range from legal recognition and an end to infanticide and non-consensual surgeries to equal access to healthcare, education and work, and a real say in decisions that affect us, alongside a call for an African intersex rights framework. Meeting openly, as gatherings like ours are criminalised across the continent, was itself a statement.


It mattered that we met in Kenya, whose census showed why being counted matters. Who a state refuses to count, it can pretend does not exist. Yet this win must be built on, because Kenya’s

Intersex Persons Bill, 2024

 has yet to

become law

.


Who decides who we are, and which children are protected?


During the conference, one question kept coming up. Who gets to decide who is intersex? There are dozens of intersex variations, and many people never know until they are tested. Yet the first response is often, “What shows you are intersex?” Demanding medical proof leaves the power to define us with medical and state systems, not with intersex people ourselves.


I hear the question, “What are you?” most often in hospitals, from family members and communities, where people feel entitled to question bodies they do not understand. Often, these probing questions determine whether you receive medical care or can use services freely accessible to others. It creates shame, fear and self-doubt, turning spaces meant to offer care and belonging into places of rejection.


The cost of not fitting is real.

Policy guidance

 from the Africa Intersex Movement and the UN Development Programme documents these harms across the continent. In Ghana, we have witnessed the same infanticide and abandonment of babies seen as a curse, children operated on to make them fit, and adults hiding their identities from their own families.


In that room, we listened and held space for one another. Every variation is unique, yet people hold fixed expectations of what an intersex person looks like. Intersex people must define who we are.


In Ghana, an opening and its limits


In Ghana, intersex people lack legal recognition and protection. Last year, with support from traditional leaders (queen mothers) and lawyers, we urged

the Constitution Review Committee

 to ban non-consensual surgeries and infanticide and recognise intersex people. The president’s white paper supported …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure

author: Soreti Kadir
title: The city beneath the capital
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial center of Addis Ababa. As I was only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine.

Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation turned to our relationship to “Ethiopia” as a national identity. I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the

Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia

 and the official establishment of a transitional government.

This eventually led to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front, among others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.

I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, colored by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections overly nostalgic, antagonistic toward the country’s future, and unconcerned with its good. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating.

That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the state looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day — discussing the political reality of our country.

Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from full-fledged conversations, opting for quiet inquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia.

Other parts of the country carry their own nuances and political realities, which deserve their own analysis; my focus here is the capital, Addis Ababa. That afternoon at the cafe points to something larger: in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair — of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance, which has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city can hold, and of the legacy of what can only be described as settler colonialism. “Where,” figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? It must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and historically different, and with a capacity unique unto itself to ground and lead us to new political possibilities.

author: Justin Hardy
title: Child welfare dispute in Peguis First Nation in Manitoba sparks lockdown
content:
A dispute over the leadership and operations of Peguis First Nation’s Child and Family Services escalated Thursday with community members, the chief and a councillor gathering outside the agency’s main office and chaining its doors shut.


The protest started Nov. 19 amid calls for changes to the agency’s leadership on the reserve located 200 km north of Winnipeg on the Interlake Region of Manitoba.


“Despite my attempts in the past to speak up for membership, there has been complete disregard for me as the chief of our nation, complete disregard for the concerns identified by members, and complete disregard for the safety and wellbeing of our children and our families,” Chief Stan Bird said in a video posted to social media in the days leading up to the protest.


RCMP officers arrived and spoke with the group. Bird has previously said he wants the band to take control of the CFS agency and reassert its inherent jurisdiction over child welfare.


He has also raised concerns about child safety and the agency’s operations.


Bird has not responded to further requests for comment.


Peguis CFS responded by announcing that its main office was in lockdown following Thursday’s incident.


“The agency is an essential service provider to Peguis members and wants to ensure to members that programs and services will continue as normal,” the announcement on their website read.


The dispute has also exposed disagreements within the community over how the agency should be governed and who should have authority over its operations.


Four of the community’s six councillors issued a notice to the community dated Nov. 21, condemning the protest, they said, was led by Bird and that that a quorum of council is needed to make any changes to the agency.


As of Nov. 25, the situation remains unresolved, with questions surrounding the agency’s leadership, its financial accountability and the future of child and family services in Peguis.


A band meeting was held in Peguis on Nov. 24. Media were not allowed in. Bird has called a news conference in Winnipeg on Thursday.


We will have more on that in the coming days.
