author: ROAPE
title: A demand that can be checked
content:
Africa is not poor. Africa is drained. What changed for the generation that filled Nairobi’s streets in 2024 was not courage but the ability to prove it.


I was raised inside a sentence. Before I could find my grandparents’ country on a map, I had been handed a verdict: it was poor. The word arrived with the settled cadence of fact, and it lodged so early that I mistook it for a thing I had discovered rather than a thing I had been given.


What broke the sentence was not a feeling. It was a number. The continent I had been taught to grieve over is not a debtor to the world. It is a creditor. More wealth leaves it each year than arrives. I had accepted that poverty the way one accepts weather. Weather has no author. A transaction has two parties.


A generation is now doing the arithmetic in public, and it has begun to ask who the other party is.


That question travels further than the ledger. It begins as arithmetic: whose wealth leaves, and by what route. It becomes politics the moment enough people can do that arithmetic at once, which is what happened in Nairobi in June 2024. And it arrives, finally, at the governments that have taken up the same grievance and answered it by making the arithmetic impossible to check. Nairobi and Ouagadougou are not two subjects. They are the same demand at two different stages of what happens when it is made.


The lie and the ledger


Across most of the colonized continent, a child was taught a single proposition: Africa is poor, as though penury were a fact of the soil rather than a condition imposed on it. The word arrived early and without cease, in the textbook, the telethon, the appeal letter. Poor Africa. It was the first sentence the world pronounced over its people, and it was a falsehood, an inversion so total that once seen, it cannot be unseen.


One fact undoes it. In 2015, a high-level panel convened jointly by the African Union and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, chaired by Thabo Mbeki, reported that

Africa loses on the order of fifty billion United States dollars each year to illicit financial flows

. The money is spirited out through trade misinvoicing, transfer mispricing, and outright theft, most of it effected by multinational corporations. Mbeki stated the arithmetic without embellishment: “The continent is losing an estimated US $50 billion a year through illicit capital outflows. This amount of money is larger in volume than the assistance the continent receives annually.”


The panel’s estimate rested on trade misinvoicing alone, the gap between customs records for the same shipment on each side of a border. A later UNCTAD accounting used a broader methodology, adding capital flight and criminal proceeds to the same trade data. It put the annual loss at

$88.6 billion, 3.7 percent of Africa’s GDP, with a cumulative total of $836 billion between 2000 and 2015

.


The abstraction “illicit financial flows” conceals how ordinary the theft is: not the suitcase of cash but the routine of commercial mispricing. A subsidiary in Lusaka or Kinshasa sells its ore to a related company abroad at a fraction of market value. The profit settles in a low-tax jurisdiction while the producing country records a loss on wealth that was demonstrably its own. Each transaction is individually deniable, papered with defensible transfer prices, so a systematic drain presents itself as a thousand unrelated, lawful-looking transfers. Estimates built on mirrored trade statistics are themselves debated among economists, and the panel’s figure is best read as an order of magnitude rather than a ledger line.


The poverty, then, is real but not native. It is manufactured: the classic paradox of plenty, in which the ground beneath the poorest villages holds the minerals the wealthy world cannot function without, and the wealth flows outward rather than up. Africa is not poor; Africa is drained. The entire moral theatre of the preceding century – the rescue, the aid, the loan – has depended upon the colonized believing the first sentence rather than the second. This is coloniality in its economic register: the extractive periphery maintained long after the flag has changed, its dispossession renamed as assistance.


The paradox of plenty


To speak of a resource curse risks the fatalism the inversion is meant to dispel: the suggestion that mineral wealth simply ruins whatever it touches, a law of nature no one need answer for.

Terry Lynn Karl’s study of oil booms …

author: Daron Letts
title: Kugluktuk welcomes 10 new modular housing units
content:
Kugluktuk’s housing stock increased by 10 modular public housing units this week.


Built by Arctic Modular Homes out of Cambridge Bay, the dwellings are a mix of three duplexes and two-, three- and four-bedroom units.


“It’s nice to finally see we are getting development in our community,” said Dettrick Hokanak, the hamlet’s deputy chief administrative officer who, in his previous role as the planning and lands administrator, approved the project.


The modular homes stem from an agreement

reached in January

 between the federal and territorial government and Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. to build up to 750 homes across the territory, including public, affordable and supportive.


Build Canada Homes is providing up to $250 million, and the territorial government is contributing up to $230 million under the agreement.


Construction and development is underway on an additional 139 homes in other communities including Iqaluit, Cambridge Bay, Arviat, Baker Lake and Rankin Inlet.


Housing Minister Cecile Nelvana Lyall and other territorial ministers attended a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Tuesday for the modular homes.


Nunavut MP Lori Idlout said in a news release on Tuesday that the development won’t solve overcrowding in the hamlet, but it’s a start.


“Ten new public housing units will not solve our housing challenge overnight,” she said. “But for 10 families, everything changes. They soon will have a safe and comfortable home to raise their families.”


Hokanak said he expects families to move in this week.


In addition, a 12-plex and two other units are under construction, headed by Concentric Associates International Inc., which has offices across Canada, including Iqaluit.


In light of Nunavut’s

housing crisis

, those units can’t come fast enough, Hokanak said.


“There could be 15 people in a three-bedroom house and 12 people in a two-bedroom house. People move from house to house,” he said.


The overcrowding takes a toll on family relationships, he said.


“It causes tension and leads to many different negative aspects of life,” he said. “I really want my community to succeed, and I really want my community members to succeed. Housing is vital.”

author: C.J. Polychroniou
title: Affordability Worries Go Beyond Prices. Addressing Them Demands Systemic Change.
content:
We must increase workers’ resources and limit capitalists’ and elites’ political power, says economist Gerald Epstein.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

“Affordability” was the buzzword of the 2026 midterm elections, echoed often by Democrats as they scored a massive victory and captured both chambers of Congress. Indeed, the cost of living was the top issue on the mind of voters as they headed to the ballot box, according to polls. But the increasing economic pressure on working-class people is also inextricably linked in voters’ mind with corruption and the war on Iran. Now, as Democrats get ready to put forth new policies under their new majorities, it still isn’t exactly clear what a focus on “affordability” actually means.

As renowned progressive economist Gerald Epstein points out in the interview that follows, “affordability” is more than prices. The “affordability crisis” points to a plethora of economic and political ills facing the contemporary United States that need to be thoroughly addressed in order to make average citizens thrive. These include extreme wealth concentration, government corruption, corporate greed and unaccountability, an out-of-control health care system, unfair tax policy, and bloated military spending. Epstein argues that the policies to address these economic and social ills are already well-known, and only political will is needed to fix the broken system.

Epstein is professor of economics and co-director of the Political Economy Research Institute (PERI) at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of the project called Game Changers: Economic Policies for a Working America.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

C. J. Polychroniou: The 2026 midterm elections have been interpreted as a referendum on President Donald Trump as voters worried about the state of the economy under his administration. In fact, “affordability” was the dominant issue in the election cycle as many people in the U.S. are struggling with the cost of housing, groceries, and health care, and worry about their financial prospects, all while the rich continue to get richer. Do you agree with this interpretation of the midterm elections? Moreover, what do we mean by “affordability” and how is it to be addressed?

Gerald Epstein: I do agree. The 2026 midterm elections could indeed be dubbed the “affordability” midterms. Poll after poll, both before and after the elections, identified the rise in the cost of living due to Trump’s Iranian adventure and romance with tariffs as the top concerns of voters. And close to the top was voters’ dissatisfaction with the corruption of Trump, his family, and his minions. In fact, corruption did not rise to the top of voters’ priorities until Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff effectively tied Trump’s corruption to American families’ affordability problems. And now that Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, they seem to be converging on a two-pronged strategy: promote legislation that will improve “affordability” and investigate the Trump administration’s corruption.

All of this raises several questions: What is meant by “affordability?” What are the policy tools available to the government at the federal but also state and local levels that could make life more affordable for Americans? And, finally, is this “affordability agenda” sufficient to address the multiple challenges facing U.S. workers?

There are many “affordability” agendas to choose from. The Congressional Progressive Caucus released a “New Affordability Agenda” in April. According to the caucus: “The New Affordability Agenda is a slate of creative new bills to help families get ahead by making things cheaper, putting money in pockets and getting big money out of politics.” The agenda includes policies such as making prescription drugs cheaper by making it easier to produce generic drugs; reducing grocery prices by reducing grocery chain monopolies; making housing more affordable by increasing rental assistance and assistance for down payments; levying windfall profits tax on oil to be returned to consumers; limiting AI’s use in dynamic pricing of products; setting a minimum of two weeks paid vacation for workers; raising federal overtime pay; and getting money out of politics by limiting super PACs.

Clearly, this is not a comprehensive agenda, but it …

author: Ana Naomi De Sousa
title: ‘No Dignified Way to Live’: Why Portugal Is Rising up Over Housing
content:
Edmilson Tavares Fonseca didn’t join the thousands of people who marched through Lisbon last Saturday to protest against Portugal’s rising living costs and unaffordable housing. Saturday is the only day he gets to spend with his partner and their baby. The rest of the week, he works two jobs, trying to make ends meet. Still, he identifies strongly with the protesters. “The people in the streets right now are demanding what most people in Portugal want,” he says. “The government have shut their eyes to reality – but we don’t have a dignified way to live right now.” 


Fonseca grew up in the Lisbon suburb of Cova da Moura, known for its precarious self-built housing. He still works full-time in the area, supporting marginalised young people, but goes home to a different part of the city, where he lives in a rented apartment with his partner. They can afford it, for now, but since becoming parents, and with average rents in the city having almost doubled since 2017, Fonseca and his partner long for the security of owning their own home. Fonseca took a second job as an Uber driver to supplement his income, but, despite this, he has been refused a mortgage four times. “Sometimes it feels as if all the sacrifices I’m making are for nothing,” he says, “it’s so demoralising”.


Fonseca’s story shows what Portugal’s housing crisis means for ordinary people. Since 2015, house prices

have outstripped wage growth by 60%

 – by far the widest gap in the EU, where the average is 6.8%. Meanwhile, public housing makes up less than 2% of the country’s housing stock.


Last weekend’s protest marked five weeks of people in Portugal taking to the streets over the housing crisis. Spontaneous

encampments have sprung up from Porto to Lisbon

, and tens of thousands have turned out to weekly demonstrations,

defying violence

 and disparagement from the authorities. As the gaping discrepancy between house prices and wages pushes both renting and buying far beyond what most can afford, people in Portugal are starting to question where all the money has gone – and who really owns the cities they live in.


“What we’re seeing now is the failure of public policies to respond to national housing needs over several decades, resulting in a deep-rooted crisis,” says Ana Cordeiro Santos, an economist at Coimbra University. 


After property prices crashed during the 2011 debt crisis, the government responded to a shortage of capital and widespread urban decay by courting foreign investment in real estate, Cordeiro Santos says. A central pillar of this strategy was the Golden Visa scheme, which offered residency – and eventually a route to citizenship to non-EU nationals who invested at least €500,000 (£420,000) in property.

 Between 2012 and 2023, it brought in €6.5bn in property investment, with most visas going to Chinese (43%), Brazilian (10%) and United States (6%) nationals, fuelling further speculation in real estate.


The flood of global capital has generated huge profits for investors, but

 made the housing market

completely unaffordable

 for ordinary Portuguese people. In Lisbon, the average net salary is currently €1,405 (£1,190) a month – while the average one-bedroom flat rents for around €1,450 (£1,230).


Frederico Ascensão da Natividade Prazeres, a 24-year-old software engineer, says he “made all the sensible choices” – and now feels “deeply betrayed”. Despite earning €2,200 (£1,860) a month, a high salary in Portugal, especially for his age, he can’t afford to live alone in the Lisbon neighbourhood where he grew up. Instead, he rents a room in a shared three-bedroom apartment with no living room, splitting his time between his bedroom and the kitchen. “I live like a rat,” he says.


He checks property websites every couple of weeks, but would have to move at least 80km away to buy. Now he’s thinking of going further – to Switzerland. Portugal’s Emigration Observatory estimates that around 65,000 people left the country in 2024. “There is an urban exodus of people of my generation,” Prazeres says. “We really don’t want to leave, but we feel we have no choice.”


So many young people are leaving Portugal just as it has become one of Europe’s most desirable destinations. Tourist overnight stays have more than doubled since 2012, helped by the deregulation of the rental market, tax breaks for short-term lets on platforms such as Airbnb, and budget airlines like easyJet and Ryanair. “Tourism has boosted the economy, but it has had …

author: anred
title: La organización de vecinos contra el olvido y la estafa logró frenar los desalojos en barrio La Merced
content:
Tras varios días de protestas, cortes de calles y una feroz represión policial que incluyo heridos y menores detenidos, los vecinos del barrio La Merced, en la localidad bonaerense de San Vicente, consiguieron un acuerdo que compromete al Municipio a intervenir en el histórico conflicto por la vivienda. El acta contempla un relevamiento integral de los terrenos, el reconocimiento de las situaciones posesorias, el impulso de un procedimiento de expropiación y gestiones para frenar los desalojos. La organización barrial logró poner en movimiento a un Estado que permanecia ausente frente al reclamo de las familias. Por ANRed


Algunos vecinos comenzaron a vaciar y derribar sus casas ante el inminete desalojo, otras decidieron que se encadenarían a las garrafas antes que perder sus casas. La situación se tornaba dramatica ante la falta de respuesta y un juicio ya concretado que exigía desalojar 17 manzanas con la posibilidad de extenderse a otras 43. Al mismo tiempo la asamblea vecinal había organizado acciones decisivas. Después de jornadas de movilización, guardias nocturnas, cortes de calles, asambleas y una brutal represión policial, se alcanzó un acuerdo que compromete al Municipio de San Vicente a intervenir en el conflicto dominial y habitacional que amenaza a cientos de familias.


El acuerdo llega después de días de extrema tensión. La Policía Bonaerense reprimió a los vecinos que reclamaban una solución, disparó balas de goma, golpeó a manifestantes y amenazó incluso con armas de fuego. También fueron detenidos dos menores de edad, que posteriormente recuperaron la libertad. Durante los operativos hubo numerosos heridos y denuncias por el accionar violento de las fuerzas de seguridad.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida de Agencia de Noticias Red Acción (@anredaccion)


 


De un supuesto conflicto entre privados a miles de familias afectadas


En medio del conflicto, el intendente de San Vicente, Nicolás Mantegazza, fue entrevistado por Radio con Vos, donde inicialmente caracterizó la situación como «un conflicto entre privados» por unas viviendas. Sin embargo, el propio desarrollo de los acontecimientos dejó en evidencia una dimensión muy diferente: no se trataba de una disputa aislada entre particulares, sino de una problemática que involucra a miles de familias y se extiende sobre más de 60 manzanas.


Frente a esa dimensión, el jefe comunal reconoció la necesidad de intervenir. Los vecinos, en diálogo con ANRed, polemizaron con las declaraciones del intendente y cuestionaron que durante años fueron ignorados por las autoridades municipales, pese a los reiterados reclamos y a la gravedad de la situación dominial y habitacional. «Muchos de los vecinos y vecinas del barrio son empleados municipales esperamos que esta situación no afecte su puesto laboral», nos comentaron.


La intervención institucional, señalaron, no surgió de una iniciativa preventiva del gobierno municipal, sino que llegó después de que las familias se organizaran, salieran a las calles y enfrentaran la amenaza concreta de perder sus viviendas.


Además, el conflicto no es nuevo. En 2021 ya se había atravesado una situación similar, con reclamos vecinales por la incertidumbre sobre la titularidad de los terrenos y el riesgo de perder las viviendas. La reiteración del problema expone la falta de respuestas de fondo durante años y el abandono de las familias frente a un entramado de operaciones inmobiliarias y disputas dominiales.


Represión y detenciones durante la protesta de los vecinos estafados en el barrio La Merced en San Vicente


 


Un acuerdo que pone al Estado frente a su responsabilidad


Entre los principales puntos del acta firmada, el Municipio se comprometió a realizar, junto con los vecinos, un relevamiento integral, técnico, catastral, dominial y ocupacional de todos los terrenos comprendidos en el conflicto. La tarea deberá identificar cada lote, sus antecedentes de titularidad, situación judicial y posesoria, así como a las familias que actualmente los habitan.


Uno de los aspectos centrales es el reconocimiento de la documentación que poseen los vecinos. El Municipio deberá recibir y evaluar los boletos de compraventa, cesiones de derechos, constancias de entrega de posesión, pagos de impuestos y servicios, construcciones y demás elementos que permitan acreditar la relación de cada familia con el terreno.


Este punto resulta fundamental en un conflicto atravesado por operaciones …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Ley de Tierras: vía libre para desalojos exprés y un Congreso a medida del extractivismo
content:
OPINIÓN


Por Silvina Ramírez*


Finalmente, se sancionó la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada. El Senado la convirtió en ley, luego de múltiples avatares que tuvieron su epicentro en la extranjerización de la tierra. La derogación de un artículo del polémico DNU 70/23, que eliminó la Ley de Tierras Rurales —la que impuso un límite a la extranjerización— fue el punto de partida de un enorme debate público que culminó con esta última sanción.


El bochornoso papel de la

Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación

, que en el lapso de diez días puso en vigencia el artículo en cuestión suspendiendo una medida cautelar, y luego en un golpe de timón volvió a establecer dicha medida prohibiendo otra vez la extranjerización, concluye en un acto final de sanción de una ley que incluye la restitución de la Ley 26.737 de tierras rurales.


Sintetizar en un párrafo las idas y vueltas parlamentarias y las decisiones de la Corte Suprema no fue una tarea fácil. Sí traduce el nivel de “tironeo” político, las negociaciones desenfrenadas, decisiones judiciales de la máxima instancia del país inexplicables, y la relevancia de

la movilización

 de diversos sectores sociales que presionaron para preservar la soberanía. En pocas palabras,

se logró la restitución de una ley que protege el territorio de la injerencia externa

.


Sin embargo, la movilización popular no alcanzó para frenar los desalojos exprés y la restricción para las expropiaciones, que subsisten en el texto de la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la propiedad privada aprobada. Estas medidas perjudican a vastos sectores de la sociedad, entre ellos las comunidades indígenas.


Los desalojos apuntan tanto a inmuebles urbanos como rurales. Al agilizar el proceso y acortar los plazos, la fragilidad de aquellos potenciales desalojados se agudiza. En el caso de las comunidades indígenas, la seguidilla de desalojos o intentos de desalojos que se dieron en los últimos meses —algunos de ellos pudieron ser suspendidos—, bajo la vigencia de esta ley, adquieren mayor gravedad.


Es el caso también de las expropiaciones. Aquellas comunidades indígenas que tienen expectativas de recuperar sus territorios a través de un procedimiento administrativo como lo es la expropiación, van a encontrar ahora muchas más dificultades, por lo que una de las vías posibles de titulación colectiva encuentra nuevos obstáculos. Nada es fácil para las comunidades indígenas que pretenden gozar de sus derechos territoriales reconocidos.


Esta ley debe leerse a la luz de otras medidas de este Gobierno que privilegian no sólo la propiedad privada, sino las inversiones extranjeras, despreciando e invisibilizando el reclamo legítimo de las comunidades indígenas, campesinos y trabajadores rurales, entre ortos. El

Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI)

, la derogación de la

Ley 26.160 (Emergencia Territorial Indígena)

, el

desguace de la Ley de Glaciares

, el rol nefasto del Instituto Nacional de Asuntos Indígenas (INAI), son

piezas de una maquinaria al servicio de la explotación de los bienes comunes naturales y el despojo

, otra vez, de los territorios indígenas.


Es cierto que se logró frenar la extranjerización de la tierra, debido principalmente a la presión ciudadana. No obstante, los objetivos de esta gestión de gobierno son claros. Muchas veces se retrocede para avanzar con mayor fuerza. Es imprescindible estar alertas frente a potenciales avances que pretendan erosionar aún más la ya débil institucionalidad pública y seguir socavando derechos que costaron tanto obtener. Que la arena (o la cal) no tape la cal (o la arena).


*

Especialista en Derechos Indígenas. Docente de la Facultad de Derecho de la UBA. Miembro de la Asociación de Abogados/as de Derecho Indígena (AADI).


La entrada

Ley de Tierras: vía libre para desalojos exprés y un Congreso a medida del extractivismo

 se publicó primero en

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Regional leaders say future of Aurora College campuses remains unclear
content:
For the last two years, Dana Fergusson has been asking Aurora College the same questions.


As chair of Thebacha Leadership Council, she wants to know what academic programs will be offered at the college’s Fort Smith and Inuvik campuses as the institution works toward becoming a polytechnic university.


She also wants to know how decisions about program locations are being made, what progress the college has made toward its transformation and how much the process has cost.


“Where are the measurable outcomes on where they are with getting closer to this polytech?” Fergusson said in an interview with APTN News. “And then tell me where the money went.”


The Thebacha Leadership Council is governed by local leadership from Salt River First Nation, Tthebatthie Denesuline Nation, Fort Smith Métis Council and Town of Fort Smith.


On Nov. 18, the council sent a second open letter to Aurora College’s board of governors, the minister of Education, Culture and Employment and all members of the legislative assembly.


The letter asks the college to make clear commitments on regional program delivery, including transparent criteria for deciding where programs are offered, an assessment of campus infrastructure and utilization, and in-person engagement with communities.


It also calls for a public plan to maintain and renew student residences.


The letter follows a presentation the council made to the board on Oct. 2.


“We just received their response letter from that, and it really felt like a nothing letter,” she said. “It had nothing of substance in it.”


The letters signed by Fergusson on behalf of the Town of Fort Smith, along with the Fort Smith Métis Council, Salt River First Nation and Thebacha Denesųłiné Nation.


Fort Smith questions the future of its campus


The concern has a longer history. A 2018 foundational review found the school needed to evolve to better meet the need of northerners and it proposed moving the college’s headquarters to Yellowknife as part of its transformation into a polytechnic university.


The Thebacha Campus has classrooms, laboratories, a library, computer labs and student housing. Fergusson said much of that infrastructure is being underutilized.


“We have this huge regional campus here, big classrooms, library, labs, computer labs, all of these resources sitting here empty, vacant,” she said.


Fergusson has started making videos to show residents what is available at the campus, including its student housing.


“Why are we talking about centralizing something in another region, another community to build all this infrastructure when you have it already sitting here in Fort Smith?” she said.


Fergusson said Fort Smith has gradually lost access to programs that once brought students to the community, including teacher education, social work and early childhood education. She said some of those programs have been absent for about eight years.


The impact, she argued, reaches beyond the classroom. Fewer students living in Fort Smith also means fewer customers for local businesses.


The uncertainty is particularly difficult for young people trying to plan their education.


Fergusson said high school students have asked how they are supposed to prepare for post-secondary studies when they do not know where a program will be delivered.


“You don’t know where it’s going to be, so you can’t plan for the community,” she said. “How do you plan for where you’re going to live?”


Students may need to arrange housing, employment and financial assistance well before a program begins. Without knowing where a course of study will be offered, Fergusson says, those decisions become harder to make.


Inuvik wants more in-person diploma programs


The concerns are not limited to Fort Smith.


In Inuvik, Mayor Peter Clarkson said the town wants more in-person programming at the Aurora College campus.


Clarkson said there’s a notable decline in student enrolment. He puts the numbers at about 165 students at one point, compared with roughly 25 more recently, and just half of that number graduating last year.


Clarkson says office and business administration courses have been offered in Inuvik for decades, alongside some upgrading and online learning.


But he wants the college to introduce more diploma programs that respond to employment needs across the Beaufort Delta and the wider territory.


His suggestions include information technology, recreation leadership, northern natural resource …

content:
Ανταπόκριση από Παρίσι. Ηρώ Σιαφλιάκη


Ένα μυστικό θαύμα συμβαίνει αυτήν την εποχή, στη σκιά της γνωστής γαλλικής εξέγερσης, όχι ως εξαίρεση αλλά ως συνέχεια, ως καρδιά θα μπορούσαμε να πούμε, παλιότερων εξεγέρσεων που η Ιστορία των γεγονότων συνήθως ξεχνά. Οι καθηγητές έκαναν μάθημα πίσω από τα κάγκελα και οι φοιτητές

τούς άκουγαν

 από την άλλη πλευρά,

 

στον δρόμο.

author: Mag
title: „Die Kürzungen sind unerträglich“: Ein breites Bündnis hat den Kampf zur Verteidigung des öffentlichen Bildungswesens in Madrid aufgenommen
content:
Dossier


„

Mehr als 20 Organisationen haben sich zusammengeschlossen, um zu versuchen, das, was sie als Plan der Regionalregierung zur Dekapitalisierung des öffentlichen Bildungswesens zugunsten des privaten Bildungswesens ansehen, rückgängig zu machen. Mit dem Ruf „Bildungsqualität oder unbefristeter Streik“ haben Tausende von Menschen heute Morgen im Zentrum der Hauptstadt mehr Mittel für die öffentliche Bildung in Madrid gefordert. An der von mehr als 20 Organisationen, darunter Gewerkschaften, Universitätsversammlungen und verschiedene soziale Gruppen, organisierten Demonstration nahmen Vertreter und konkrete Forderungen aus allen Bildungsbereichen, von den 0- bis 3-Jährigen bis zu den Studenten und der Berufsausbildung, sowie politische Parteien teil. Nach Angaben der Organisatoren nahmen etwa 120.000 Menschen an der Demonstration teil

…“ So beginnt der umfangreiche span.

Artikel von Guillermo Martínez vom 23. Februar 2025 in elDiario.es


 (maschinenübersetzt) mit schönen Fotos der Transparente – siehe mehr Infos:


Die Lehrkräfte in der 7. Woche des unbefristeten Bildungsstreiks in Madrid kämpfen nach Verschärfung der Mindestdienstvorschriften auch für das Streikrecht


Madrid: Sechs Wochen Bildungsstreik, Stehversammlungen und Proteste auf der Straße gegen die Zensur


„

Die Lehrkräfte beenden die Woche vom 16. bis 20. November mit dem Einsatz für Verhandlungsrechte und das Streikrecht angesichts der Verschärfung der Mindestdienstvorschriften und der Anweisungen des Bildungsministeriums. Die Organisation an den Schulen sowie die Zusammenarbeit mit den Kindergärten und der Universität tragen einen Kampf aus, der sich nicht auf die Wände des Klassenzimmers beschränken lässt. Die sechste Woche des unbefristeten Streiks im öffentlichen Bildungswesen Madrids hinterlässt ein Bild, das den Konflikt auf den Punkt bringt: Lehrkräfte versammeln sich vor dem Bildungsministerium, einige mit Aufklebern über den Lippen, um gegen die Einschränkungen ihres Protests zu protestieren; dabei beteiligen sich auch Schüler und es wird gefordert, dass Mercedes Zarzalejo Verhandlungen aufnimmt.


Zwei Wochen nach der

in LoQueSomos veröffentlichten Bilanz der vierten Woche


 bleiben die Kernpunkte des Konflikts bestehen: Senkung der Schüler-Lehrer-Verhältnisse und der Unterrichtsbelastung, Aufstockung des Personals und stärkere Berücksichtigung der Vielfalt, Wiederherstellung der Kaufkraft sowie die Bereitstellung angemessener Schulgebäude. Es gibt keine Einigung, die den am 14. Oktober begonnenen Streik beenden würde. Doch diese Woche kommt ein Thema hinzu, das untrennbar mit diesen Forderungen verbunden ist: die Verteidigung der kollektiven Mittel, mit denen die Lehrkräfte diese Forderungen durchsetzen. (…)


Die Versammlungen – die Arbeit, die die Straße am Laufen hält


Die Mobilisierung lässt sich nicht allein durch ihre Demonstrationen erklären. Es gibt ein Netzwerk der täglichen Organisation, das die Aktionen vorbereitet, die nächsten Schritte bespricht und die Probleme der einzelnen Zentren mit einem gemeinsamen Forderungskatalog verknüpft. „Menos Lectivas“ beschreibt seine Struktur anhand souveräner Zentrumsversammlungen, die im Konsens oder durch Abstimmung entscheiden und über Verbindungsleute verfügen, um ihre Positionen an die Generalversammlung weiterzuleiten. Die territorialen Versammlungen ermöglichen die Koordination von Schulen innerhalb desselben Stadtviertels oder Gebiets; die Gruppen nach Schulstufen und Fachbereichen machen unterschiedliche Bedürfnisse sichtbar. (…)


Vom Haushalt in Vallecas bis zum Druck auf die regionalen Behörden


Am Dienstag, dem 17., versammelten sich Hunderte von Lehrkräften vor dem Regionalparlament von Madrid, während Zarzalejo den Haushalt seines Ministeriums verteidigte. Die Sprecherinnen des Komitees legten in der nahegelegenen Buchhandlung Muga ihre Sicht auf den Haushalt dar: Die Gesamtsteigerung reicht nicht aus, wenn sie sich nicht in mehr Lehrkräften, geringeren Schülerzahlen pro Klasse, öffentlichen Stellen und Infrastruktur niederschlägt. Angesichts der offiziellen Präsentation von Rekordzahlen stellte der Protest die entscheidende Frage: Was kommt tatsächlich in den öffentlichen Klassenzimmern an?.

author: Rigaer94
title: Rigaer94: Ah shit, here we go again.
content:
Für den Text auf anderen Sprachen schaut auf unseren Blog (https://rigaer94.squat.net/2026/11/20/rigaer94-ah-shit-here-we-go-again/)


Es ist mal wieder ernst. Noch diesen Sommer haben wir davon berichtet, dass einige Räumungstitel gegen Wohnungen in unserem Haus bestehen: (

https://rigaer94.squat.net/2026/05/10/all-out-for-the-defense-of-rigaer94/

)


“Wie wir letztes Jahr berichtet haben, sind die zwischen den alten Mietvertragsinhaber*innen und den selbsternannten Anwälten Bernau und Aretin des angeblichen Eigentümers (Leonid Medved) zwar nicht formell, aber faktisch, Räumungstitel. Diese kommen zu den zwei bereits aus den letzten Jahren existierenden Räumungstiteln hinzu, was bedeutet das es jetzt insgesamt acht Räumungstitel im Haus gibt. In den letzten Monaten haben unsere Gegner einige Räumungsklagen zurückgezogen, die für sie aussichtslos wirkten. Obwohl dadurch einige Individuen aus den Räumungsklagen raus sind, sind das für uns keine guten Neuigkeiten – vielmehr macht es ein Räumungsszenario wahrscheinlicher, da es bald keine offenen Klagen, sondern nur noch Räumungstitel geben wird.”


Letzte Woche Mittwoch, am 11. November, gab es wieder einen Verhandlungstermin zu diesen Räumungsklagen. In der Verhandlung machte der Richter erneut deutlich, dass er keineswegs plant, die Lafone Investments Limited als rechtsfähig anzuerkennen. Noch während der Verhandlung zogen die Anwälte des vermeintlichen Eigentümers dann auch die letzten aussichtslosen Klagen gegen diejenigen Individuen zurück, die nicht in Verbindung mit Mietverträgen stehen. Das scheint ihre aktuelle Strategie zu sein: Den Weg für eine Teilräumung zu ebnen. Und heute sehen wir auch, was genau das bedeutet:


Innerhalb der letzten Tage haben wir vier Räumungsankündigungen erhalten. Drei davon resultieren aus den Deals der alten Mietvertragsinhaber*innen mit den selbsternannten Anwälten. Eine der Räumungsankündigungen basiert auf einem bereits länger existierenden Räumungstitel. Bisher wissen wir also sicher, dass es vier Wohnungen betrifft. Wir müssen aber davon ausgehen, dass zu den vier weiteren Wohnungen auch noch Räumungsankündigungen eintreffen werden.


Die Obergerichtsvollzieherin Frau Knop (Segelfliegerdamm 89 12487 Berlin, Tel.03091693556) hat sich für den 15.12.26 um 06:00 Uhr morgens angekündigt, um die ehemaligen Mietvertragsinhaber*innen aus den Wohnungen zu räumen und die vermeintlichen Eigentümer*innen in diese “einzuweisen”.


Was treiben die Behörden da?


Wir fragen uns, ob die Ankündigung der Gerichtsvollzieherin eine rein bürokratische Angelegenheit ist, oder ob Bullen und Politik von Anfang an ihre Finger mit im Spiel haben. Es könnte ja sein, dass Frau Knop mal einen Brief losgeschickt hat, weil es einfach der übliche Verwaltungsweg ist.- ohne sich der Konsequenzen bewusst zu sein. Oder saß sie bereits mit Bernau, Aretin, einem „Eigentümer“, den Bullen und dem Innensenat an einem Tisch? Wissen dann die Hundertschaften schon Bescheid, dass sie sich auf Überstunden und Kürzungen von Urlaubstagen kurz vor Weihnachten und Silvester einstellen müssen? Oder machen die das gerne ehrenamtlich?


Falls es so ist, dass Politiker:innen bereits Bescheid wissen: Kurz vorm Sommer schien es wahrscheinlicher (

https://rigaer94.squat.net/2026/05/10/all-out-for-the-defense-of-rigaer94/

), dass ein Angriff gegen unser Haus dem CDU-geführten Senat im Berliner Wahlkampf attraktiv erschien. Die CDU hätte ihr Wahlversprechen einhalten können und sich zusammen mit Innensenatorin Iris Spranger (SPD) als Hardliner gegen links verkaufen können. Ist es jetzt der letzte Versuch einer abgewählten Regierung dem neuen Senat zu schaden bzw. ihn zu zwingen, eine Räumung zu Ende zu führen, die allen Wahlversprechen der LINKEn entgegen steht? Oder ist es der konfrontative Kurs im Kampf gegen eine Bewegung von unten, der mehr und mehr auf der Tagesordnung steht und auf den sich alle Parteien einigen können?


Schon einen Tag nach der für „Eigentümer“, Bullen und Politik gescheiterten Brandschutzbegehung im Juni 2021, war sich der SPD-Innensenat sicher, so einen Angriff nicht wiederholen zu wollen: “Mit der Ramme rein ins Haus und alle rausholen klingt in manchen Ohren vielleicht verlockend, ist aber fern ab jeder Realität […]” (Andreas Geisel(https://berlin.t-online.de/region/berlin/id_90251346/berlin-innensenator-geisel-fuer-raeumung-von-rigaer-94-.html), ehemaliger Innensenator, Juni 2021(https://kontrapolis.info/4063/)). title: Enflasyon ve konut beklentisi geriledi, dolar tahmini yükseldi
content:
Türkiye Cumhuriyet Merkez Bankası (TCMB), kasım ayına ilişkin “Hanehalkı Beklenti Anketi” sonuçlarını açıkladı. Verilere göre, hanehalkının yıllık enflasyon ve konut fiyatı artış beklentilerinde düşüş kaydedilirken, dolar beklentisinde artış gözlendi. 12 ay sonrası yıllık enflasyon beklentisi bir önceki aya kıyasla 0,51 puan azalarak yüzde 43,24 seviyesine geriledi. Konut fiyatlarındaki artış beklentisi de, bir önceki aya göre 0,26 puan gerileyerek yüzde 30,10 oldu.

Genel enflasyon ve konut fiyatı artış beklentilerindeki gerileme karşısında, önümüzdeki 12 ay boyunca akaryakıt ve temel gıda fiyatlarının artmasının beklediğini bildirdi.

ABD Dolar kuru beklentisi ise, bir önceki aya göre 1,32 TL artış göstererek 58,18 TL seviyesine yükseldi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Amid continuing displacement, Marawi students face educational barriers
content:
The 2024 data of the Philippine Statistics Authority showed that the BARMM had the lowest basic literacy rate among all regions in the country at 81 percent. Lanao del Sur ranked third among the region’s five provinces.


MARAWI CITY, Lanao del Sur — Affecting one’s education due to financial difficulties is a typical problem of poor communities in many parts of the country. But for families displaced after the Marawi Siege in 2017, having such a problem amid their continuing displacement hits differently.


There were many occasions that the children of Nurania Unte, 33, were not able to go to school due to financial constraints. Her family is now living in Hijrah village, Barangay Sultan Corobong, a remote temporary shelter in the Islamic City of Marawi.


Nurania Unte, an internally displaced person, watches people outside her house in Hijrah village, Barangay Sultan Corobog, one of the remote temporary shelters in Marawi City. Photo by Franck Dick Rosete/Bulatlat


Her husband’s average salary in a week, ranging from P2,500 to P4,000 (approximately US$39 to $62), for working as a construction worker remains insufficient to meet their daily needs. Since it is a project-based work, there are days when the family breadwinner is jobless.


To ensure school attendance, Unte’s three children, in many instances, were forced to walk for more or less 30 minutes from their temporary shelter to the nearest Dulay Elementary School as they cannot afford the P20 fare. 


“Almost all families here have the same problem,” she told

Bulatlat

 in Filipino.


Before the five-month Marawi Siege, Unte used to live in Barangay Papandayan. The village was not part of the 24 barangays classified as most affected areas (MAA). But the lack of financial capacity to repair their house left her family with no choice but to bear the dire situation in the shelter.


Barangay Sultan Corobong, previously part of Barangay Dulay Proper, is one of the newly created villages in Marawi, following the reported increase in the population in certain areas after the siege.


The community in Hijrah village, home of reported around 1,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs), needs free transportation as the reported cost of a back-and-forth fare stood at P240 (US$3.75) going to the city proper. “The residents here don’t have stable jobs,” Nasser Dimaampo Bongcaran, the temporary shelter president, said in Filipino.


Photo shows some of the temporary housing units in Hijrah village, Barangay Sultan, Corobong, Marawi City. Photo by Franck Dick Rosete/Bulatlat


Jelilah Casarigan, mother of seven, recalled the days that her eldest daughter ended up making the sacrifice by not being able to go to school to prioritize other siblings, and she cries every time it happens.


“My child is diligent in her studies,” Casarigan, who lives in the Bakwit village, a temporary shelter in Barangay Pindolonan, Saguiaran, Lanao del Sur, told

Bulatlat

in Filipino. “Sometimes we struggle with our finances because my [construction worker] husband does not always have a job.”


The 2025 data of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) showed that Lanao del Sur registered the second highest unemployment rate among five provinces in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) at 7.99 percent, which translates to 44,000 unemployed individuals.


https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30904271/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script


Unlike the IDPs in Hiraj village, families residing in the Bakwit village, on top of the utility bills, have started paying P500 (approximately $8) for monthly rent just this year, following the eviction notice they had received from the landowner.


Read:


Displaced Marawi residents face eviction from temporary shelter


The Casarigan family was awarded a permanent shelter in Saguiaran town, a few kilometers away from Marawi City, but they have yet to transfer since there was no electricity and water connections yet. 


Same struggles


Families in permanent shelters have been dealing with the same struggles. Ibralyn Macaraguit, mother of six, gives P70 ($1.09) to one of her children studying high school a day, of which P60 ($0.98) serves as the back-and-forth fare.


The lack of local transportation also gives them headaches, leaving her child to go on foot for more or less 30 minutes from Racman Pimping Maniri Dumarpa (RPMD) National Science High School in Barangay Papandayan going to their house in Darussalam village, a …

title: Primeros Auxilios en contexto de manifestación callejera, segunda edición
content:
Movilización de jubiladxs el 24 de septiembre del año 2025. Fotografía: Andrés Manrique (ANRed).


Muchas veces, el primer objetivo de la represión es inducir temor para desairar primero y después desarticular las resistencias populares. Contra ello, ANRed libera la segunda edición de

 “Primeros Auxilios en contexto de manifestación callejera”

, una recopilación de medidas y cuidados básicos a la hora de hacernos de las calles.


Saber de primeros auxilios en contextos donde predomina la violencia puede ser un aporte muy valioso, que tiene en sí mismo un efecto tranquilizador. Además, las personas que no recibieron entrenamiento en primeros auxilios suelen dudar al momento de actuar, o tienen miedo de ayudar por falta de seguridad para recordar las maniobras.


Si bien no frenará la decisión política de mutilar, intentamos generar conciencia sobre la importancia de cuidar nuestros cuerpos, con los que trabajamos y sostenemos nuestras vidas y las de otros, y enfatizamos en aquellas cosas que sí podemos hacer para cuidarnos. En particular, esta guía está orientada a la prevención.


Recordamos que los cuidados son siempre una tarea colectiva, históricamente menospreciada pero fundamental para cualquier resistencia. Este es nuestro aporte.


Estamos hace 32 años en las calles, practicando la comunicación alternativa, comunitaria y popular. Acompañando las luchas siempre, mostrando lo que otros omiten y silencian.

author: Malik Chiconela Santana
title: Mozambique: A Judicial Solution to a Political Problem
content:
Venâncio Bila Mondlane, the leader of the Mozambican opposition, finds himself awaiting trial (scheduled for November 17) for his alleged role as the progenitor of the seismic protests that followed the 2024 elections and threatened to topple the state. Mondlane is president of the recently formed National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (ANAMOLA) party. He is accused of five crimes by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, namely

public justification of crime, incitement of collective disobedience, public instigation of crime, instigation of terrorism, and incitement of terrorism

. A conviction could mean up to 20 years in prison for the presidential runner-up, the crippling of the opposition, and a transition in the state’s handling of political opponents.


Mondlane’s road to the 2024 ballot was lined with legal and procedural obstacles.

Blocked

 from contesting the leadership of his party at the time, the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO), he left it and allied his campaign with the Democratic Alliance Coalition (CAD), whose electoral eligibility was confirmed on May 9, but was excluded by the National Election Commission (CNE) on July 18. The Constitutional Council (CC) upheld the decision on appeal, arguing that the parties who had formed CAD failed to notify the

Ministry of Justice and Constitutional and Religious Matters

 of their intention to form a coalition. The court framed the decision as a purely technical issue; however, its consequences were undeniably political. Mondlane found himself politically isolated only two months before the elections. Forced to reorganize his campaign, Mondlane forged a last-minute partnership with the Optimistic People for the Development of Mozambique (PODEMOS), running as an independent with the party’s political and parliamentary support.


This chronology illustrates how the political agency of Mondlane and his supporters was repeatedly at odds with applications of the electoral law. It may not establish that each application of electoral law was politically motivated, but, at the very least, it raises a broader question of how ostensibly procedural outcomes can reshape the field of political competition, and suggests that legal procedure is not necessarily neutral.


After the October 9, 2024, vote, the CNE declared Daniel Chapo, candidate of the ruling Mozambique Liberation Front (Frelimo), the winner with about 70%, to Mondlane’s 20%. In December, after more than 300 complaints of electoral crimes and irregularities had been lodged with local and district courts, the Constitutional Council revised those figures to roughly 65% and 24% respectively. The revision was, in effect, an admission that the election commission’s results were dubious at best and fictional at worst. The CC altered the results when, as a body of electoral oversight, it could only order the CNE to recount the votes or annul the elections. Unsurprisingly,

the Mozambican Bar Association

 (OAM), opposition parties, and civil society groups expressed concerns over the CC’s vague legal reasoning and the lack of an evidentiary basis for its alteration of the results.


What ensued in the wake of these opaque elections was a six-month period of unprecedented violence. In Mozambique, several elections have been followed by periods of armed conflict. What made this period unprecedented, however, was that the antagonism was not between the state and an organized army, but rather between the state and a mobilized mass of unarmed civilians. According to a

report

 by the Mozambican NGO Plataforma Decide, 411 civilians were killed, some 3,700 were injured, and around 7,200 were illegally detained between October 2024 and January 2025. These figures were disputed by the then commander-general of the police, Bernardino Rafael, who stated that 96 civilians were killed. Even so, charges have only been brought

against two officers

, and, with no updates, it is unclear whether the prosecution is pursuing these cases at all.


The protests began on October 21, when Mondlane called for a peaceful march in tribute to Elvino Dias, his lawyer, who was assassinated by assailants of no particular origin as he prepared an appeal challenging the preliminary election results. This march, like many that followed, was dispersed violently, including through the use of tear gas and live ammunition. In an environment where constitutionally protected political activities are met with violence, the …

author: Unknown
title: Protests in Qamişlo: 25 Rojava University students injured
content:
A total of 25 students were injured on November 16 in Qamişlo during protests against the planned incorporation of Rojava University into Syria’s state higher education system. The university’s Student Council announced the figures at a press conference on Sunday. For the first time, the council also confirmed that shots had been fired on university grounds during the crackdown. The council condemned the use of tear gas and firearms against the protesters as a serious violation of the university’s autonomy and the safety of its students.


The statement was issued on the university campus in Qamişlo in the presence of students. Mehebad Adil Serhan read it in Kurdish, while Fadiya Ebdullah read it in English. The Student Council explained that the delay in issuing the statement was due to its efforts over the past few days to care for the injured students and investigate the consequences of the events.


Dispute over the future of Rojava University


The clashes were triggered by a visit from a delegation from Damascus on Monday. The delegation held talks with the university administration about the planned incorporation of Rojava University into al-Furat University in Hesekê. Following the meeting, students demanded information about the decisions reached and the future of their university. When the delegation refused to make a statement, the students blocked its departure.


The conflict stems from two measures introduced by Syria’s transitional government. In addition to the planned incorporation of Rojava University into al-Furat University, the dispute concerns the Ministry of Education’s decision to revoke the recognition of equivalency for degrees awarded by certain faculties. Students regard these measures as an attack on their university’s independent academic and institutional identity.


The protests were therefore directed not merely against an administrative restructuring, but also against interference in academic self-governance and the students’ future. When the students insisted on receiving information about the planned changes, security forces of the transitional government attacked the protesters.


“Unjustifiable under any circumstances”


The Student Council described the actions as a serious violation of university autonomy and a direct threat to the safety and health of students. The protests, it said, had been an expression of legitimate demands and a commitment to preserving the academic and administrative independence of their university. Rather than resorting to violence, it added, those responsible should have sought dialogue and listened to the students’ concerns.


“What we witnessed on university grounds was the use of tear gas and firearms, which left 25 students injured. These shocking scenes are unacceptable under any circumstances and cannot be justified in any way,” the council stated. It condemned the use of military force, weapons, tear gas, and smoke agents on campus as “an attack on the inviolability of the educational institution and the dignity of all students.”


The statement did not specify whether the students’ injuries were caused by tear gas, gunfire, or other forms of violence.


Protection against reprisals and preservation of university autonomy


The council also strongly opposed any potential reprisals related to the protests. “We firmly reject any decision or measure aimed at arresting or prosecuting students for their participation in the peaceful defense of their rights,” the statement read. Such actions would further exacerbate tensions within the university, the Student Council warned and therefore demanded binding guarantees for students’ safety and protection against intimidation, pressure, and all forms of discrimination.


Regarding the university’s future, the council reaffirmed its commitment to preserving its academic and administrative independence. “Students must be able to voice their concerns peacefully and participate in decisions affecting their education and the university’s institutional future. We reject the imposition of decisions with far-reaching consequences without dialogue and mutual understanding,” the council declared. It also stressed that students must not be made to bear the consequences of decisions that jeopardize their academic future.


Appeal to international academic and human rights organizations


The Student Council called on international academic institutions, human rights organizations, and student representative bodies …

content:
Uluslararası İklim Eylem Ağı (Climate Action Network International-CAN), Antalya'da düzenlenen COP31'in ardından yayımladığı değerlendirmede konferansın iklim finansmanı, adil geçiş, fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşma ve iklim değişikliğine uyum konularında beklenen sonuçları vermediğini savundu.

Örgüt, iki hafta süren müzakerelerde özellikle Avrupa Birliği öncülüğündeki gelişmiş ülkelerin daha önce verilen taahhütlerin uygulanmasını engellediğini ileri sürdü. Türkiye ve Avustralya'nın konferans başkanlıklarının ise müzakereleri anlamlı sonuçlara yönlendirmekte başarısız olduğunu belirtti.

CAN Uluslararası İcra Direktörü Tasneem Essop, konferansın sonuçlarına ilişkin değerlendirmesinde, “Bu, şimdiye kadarki en kötü COP idi. İnsanların hayal bile edilemeyecek ölçekte acı çektiğine tanık oluyoruz ve bu konferansın insanları giderek ağırlaşan iklim krizinden korumak için adımlar atmasını umuyorduk. Bunun yerine zengin ülkeler, fark yaratabilecek önlemleri etkisiz hâle getirdi” ifadelerini kullandı.

Gelişmiş ülkelerin iklim kriziyle mücadele için mali kaynak sağlama yükümlülüklerinden kaçındığını savunan Essop, Avrupa Birliği'nin fosil yakıtlara ilişkin ifadelerin metinde bulunmamasını gerekçe göstererek sonuç metnine karşı çıkmasını da eleştirdi.

Essop, Avrupa ülkelerinin kendi fosil yakıt kullanımlarını sona erdirme ve gelişmekte olan ülkelere finansman sağlama yükümlülüklerini yerine getirmediğini ileri sürdü.

CAN tarafından yapılan açıklamada, COP31 başkanlıklarını yürüten Türkiye ve Avustralya'nın müzakerelerdeki tutumuna da eleştiri yöneltildi.

İki ülkenin temel müzakere başlıkları yerine kapsamlı bir genel karar metnine ağırlık verdiğini savunan örgüt, bunun iklim finansmanı, adil geçiş ve emisyon azaltımı konularındaki görüşmelerden dikkati uzaklaştırdığını öne sürdü.

Açıklamada, konferansa fosil yakıt şirketleri, karbon giderimi teknolojilerini destekleyen kuruluşlar ve yapay zekâ sektöründen çok sayıda temsilcinin katıldığı belirtildi. Karbon yakalama, kullanma ve depolama sektöründen 700 lobicinin konferansta olduğu kaydedilen açıklamada, bu teknolojilerin fosil yakıt üretiminin devam etmesine gerekçe oluşturabileceği uyarısında bulunuldu.

CAN tarafından yapılan açıklamada ayrıca, COP31'de iklim değişikliğine uyum için ayrılan finansmanın üç katına çıkarılmasına ilişkin somut bir uygulama planı oluşturulamadığı vurgulandı.

Açıklamada, gelişmekte olan ülkelerin 2035 yılına kadar iklim değişikliğine uyum için yıllık 305 milyar dolara ihtiyaç duyacağı, enflasyon dikkate alındığında bu ihtiyacın 420 milyar dolara ulaşacağı belirtildi.

Açıklamada, Paris Anlaşması'nın gelişmiş ülkelerin kamu kaynaklarından iklim finansmanı sağlamasına ilişkin 9.1 maddesinin hatırlatılmasına rağmen bu yükümlülüğün nasıl yerine getirileceğine ilişkin somut bir plan ortaya konulmadığı vurgulandı.

CAN Uluslararası Siyasi Stratejiler Başkanı Jacobo Ocharan, fosil yakıt sektörünün karbon yakalama teknolojileri üzerinden üretimini sürdürmeye çalıştığını ileri sürerek, “Konferans başkanlıklarının görevi bu müzakerelerin bütünlüğünü korumaktı. Bunun yerine kirleticilere fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşmayı geciktirmek için yeni bir gerekçe sundular” dedi.

CAN Güney Asya Direktörü Dr. Sanjay Vashist ise Türkiye ve Avustralya başkanlıklarını, fosil yakıt çıkarlarını ve zengin ülkelerin ayrıcalıklarını iklim adaletinin önüne koymakla suçladı.

CAN Enerji Dönüşümü Kıdemli Yöneticisi Janet Milongo, sonuç metninde fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşmaya ilişkin somut bir yol haritası bulunmadığını savundu. Milongo, hükümetlerin fosil yakıtları açıkça ifade etmekten kaçınırken karbon yakalama teknolojilerine geniş yer verdiğini belirterek, bunun kirletici sektörlere yeni fırsatlar sunduğunu ileri sürdü.

CAN Uyum Çalışmaları Sorumlusu Pooja Dave, COP30'da verilen finansman taahhüdünün yeniden hatırlatılmasının yeterli olmadığını ifade ederek, “Başlangıç noktası veya uygulama planı olmadan uyum finansmanını üç katına çıkarma taahhüdünü tekrarlamak hiçbir şey ifade etmiyor. Sel, kuraklık ve ölümcül sıcaklıklarla karşı karşıya kalan aileler teknik raporların arkasına sığınamaz. Her gecikme yılı hayatlara mal oluyor” dedi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Reisegruppe
title: Reisebericht Paris Herbst 2026
content:
Die Bilder einer „Klasse, die den Kopf wieder hochhebt“


Gespannt saßen wir vor unseren Geräten. „The Revolution will not be televised“, aber scheinbar „live on tiktok“. Ohne große, sichtbare Event-Mobilisierung blockieren die französischen Schüler*innen ihre Oberschulen. Auf dem fruchtbaren Boden einer langjährigen Tradition in Frankreich und einer ersten Blockade in den französischen Koloniegebieten dieses Jahr, beginnt ein Gymnasium einer Pariser Vorstadt aus Wut über die Bedingungen, die sie jeden Tag vorfinden, ihre Schule zu verbarrikadieren. Über die Verbreitung von Videos von der Aktion entsteht schnell eine landesweite Bewegung mit hunderten Nachahmer*innen, die auch die reichen Teile Frankreichs erfasst und nicht lange fackelt, den Protest mit Feuer und Militanz zu untermauern. Die Schüler*innen Frankreichs gehen in Teilen seit 2 Monaten nicht mehr zur Schule und haben sich zu einer Staatsgefährdenden Kraft entwickelt, die selbst mit 5 Milliarden des tief verschuldeten Macron-Regime nicht einzufangen ist. Das ganze steht nicht im Kontext einer Reformbestrebung oder ähnlichem sondern ist die Fortsetzung der Nahel-Revolte von 2023.


Währendessen bekommen wir von Überall aus Europa Nachrichten, wie sich junge Leute dem Aufstand der Schüler*innen anschließen und „wie in Frankreich“ protestieren, blockieren, plündern und angreifen. Wir fragen uns wann es in Deutschland los geht, ob wir als Erwachsene etwas tun können und kommen erstmal nur in Passivität. Uns erreichen die ersten Aufrufe eines Gelbwesten Revivals was mit der aktuellen GenZ-Revolte verknüpft werden soll. Die Lebenserhaltungskosten in Frankreich sind wie in Deutschland enorm gestiegen. Die Polizei hat die Schüler*innen mit allem bekämpft was wir von ihnen kennen, inklusive amputierten Händen, ausgeschossenen Augen und tausenden herabwürdigenden Festnahmen bei Minderjährigen. Dies ruft, verständlicherwise, Empörung bei allen Eltern und empathischen Menschen hervor. Das Land scheint also zu brodeln und meine Güte ist der Vulkan ausgebrochen. Hunderte Verletzte Polizt*innen, Tausende geplünderte Geschäfte und hunderttausende Beteiligte beschreiben nur im Ansatz das was dort am 17.10. an aufständiger Freude, Gemeinschaft und Power stattgefunden hat und was alle die wir getroffen haben nur als „historisch“ beschreiben konnten.


Im Kontext der letzten Geschehnisse war für uns klar, wir müssen dahin um uns selbst ein Bild von der Lage vor Ort zu verschaffen.


Als Deutsche auf einem Protest in Frankreich


An einem regnerischen Herbstag ging es früh los. Ausgerüstet mit Atemmasken, Schutzbrillen und ordentlich Proviant zog es uns in Richtung Innenstadt. Angekommen in der Nähe vom Place de la Republique suchten wir vergebens nach den viel beschriebenen aufständigen Personen. Nach einiger Zeit erfolglosem Suchen breitet sich die erste Enttäuschung in unseren Köpfe aus. Ist der Funke einer neuen Protestbewegung erloschen?


Nicht wirklich. Zum Glück konnten uns vorortig wohnende Genoss*innen Bescheid geben, dass die heutige Demo am Stadtrand noch stattfinden wird. Anscheinend hatten die heftigen Krawalle vom 17.10 dem französischen Innenminesterium so einen Schrecken eingejagt, dass sie aus Angst die Pariser Innenstadt vor jeglicher Demonstrationen schützen wollten.


Also ging es mit der U-Bahn Richtung Osten der franz. Hauptstadt. Schon am Gleis bemerkten wir, dass es um uns herum voller geworden ist. Es schien als ob ganz Paris zur Demonstrationen fahren will. Und BAM! Der Auftaktkundebungsort ist eine riesige Blase an Menschen. Man kann das Ende nur erahnen und wir kriegen Gänsehaut beim Anblick der Jugendlichen auf den Haltestelldächern und den tausenden Leute die ACAB grölen (obwohl das hier eher ACAB singen ist). Die Vorfreude steigt auf das Kommende. Nach kurzer Pinkelpause setzte sich der Protestzug in Bewegung. Es gibt keinen Punkt von dem man aus, das Ende sowie den Anfang der Demo sehen kann. Er ist schlicht zu lang. Sowas haben wir in der Form in Deutschland noch nicht erlebt. Das hier ist kein FFF-Protest, kein inhaltsloses Unteilbar-Bündnis sondern eine über 100.000 Personen-Versammlung, die eine eigene Bewegung darstellt. Zwar folgte die Mehrheit einem Aufruf der nicht-revolutionären Gewerkschaften, trotzdem ist es bewundernswert, wie sich die Aufständigen von den massiven Repressionen der letzten Wochen nicht einschüchtern lassen. Zudem stehen die heutigen Proteste als Nachfolge und in Solidarität mit den landesweiten subversiven …

author: Ezra
title: OG FFM: Aufenthaltsverbote nach den GenZ-Protesten in Frankfurt am Main
content:
OG FFM: Aufenthaltsverbote nach den GenZ-Protesten in Frankfurt am Main


Das Resümee auf Seiten der Teilnehmer*innen an den Protesten gegen soziale Ungleichheit, steigende Lebenshaltungskosten, Kürzungen im Bildungsbereich und die Wehrpflicht ist erschütternd. Viele, gerade junge Menschen, erlebten während und nach der Demonstration brutale Polizeigewalt. 

„Im Nachgang der Demonstration meldeten sich viele Betroffene bei uns und anderen Organisationen und berichteten von Verletzungen, die durch den Polizeieinsatz entstanden sind. Neben zahlreichen Augenverletzungen durch den massiven Einsatz von Pfefferspray gab es auch schwere Gehirnerschütterungen, Rippenbrüche und Knochenbrüchen“, so Anna Kaiser von der Roten Hilfe Ortsgruppe Frankfurt. 

Auch in Sozialen Medien ist einerseits das rücksichtslose Vorgehen der Polizei gegen alle Teilnehmenden der Proteste dokumentiert. Andererseits zeugen Berichte von den unbeholfenen und widersprüchlichen Polizeitaktiken vor Ort. Teilnehmende, welche den Protestzug verlassen wollten, wurden von der Polizei teilweise gewaltsam daran verhindert und kollektiv in der Frankfurter Innenstadt eingekesselt.

Einige der Protestierende erhielten in den letzten Tagen Post durch das Polizeipräsidium Frankfurt, genauer die

SOKO

 3110. Ihnen wurde ein Aufenthaltsverbot für die Frankfurter Innenstadt angedroht. 

„Nach wochenlanger medialer wie stadtpolitischer Hetze gegen die Proteste schien es Aufgabe der Polizei zu sein, Bilder der Eskalation mindestens hinzunehmen, oder sogar mit zu produzieren“, so Anna Kaiser. „Die nun folgenden Grundrechtseinschränkungen dienen dazu, die rassistische und autoritäre Hetze zu untermauern.“ Viele der Verbote sollen willkürlich bis Januar 2027 ausgesprochen werden.

Die Gewalt und die jetzigen Versuche, die geplanten Proteste gegen die Wehrpflicht am 20. November zu kriminalisieren, zeugen davon, dass die Polizei kein neutraler Akteur ist. Die Rote Hilfe empfiehlt, nicht mit der Polizei zu kooperieren, gegen Auflagen und Aufenthaltsverbote Widerspruch einzulegen und sich juristisch und politisch dagegen zu wehren.

Rote Hilfe – Ortsgruppe Frankfurt am Main


Ezra


21.11.2026 - 00:46


Pressemitteilung


Während der GenZ-Regelt-Proteste in Frankfurt am Main am 31.10.2026 erlitten dutzende, meist junge Menschen durch den brutalen Einsatz der Polizei schwere Verletzungen – vom Rippenbrüchen bis zur schweren Gehirnerschütterungen. Darüber hinaus erhielten einige Protestierende in den letzten Tagen eine schriftliche Androhung eines Aufenthaltsverbots für die Frankfurter Innenstadt. Teilweise bis Januar 2027. Die medialen Szenen, welche die Polizei mitzutragen hat, dienen nun für weitreichende repressive Grundrechtseinschränkungen.

author: Sofia Little
title: Protests Across the Pond: Gen-Z and the Fight for Affordability in Europe
content:
Across Europe, rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and underfunded public services have fueled a growing wave of protests. Since mid-September, more than 1,700 cost-of-living demonstrations have taken place in 31 European countries. The protests have brought students, workers, and community members into the streets, with young people playing a visible role in organizing and demanding change.

In France, a country with a centuries-long history of protest, the demonstrations began with students demanding more resources for underfunded schools. Students raised concerns about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and crumbling infrastructure. The demonstrations grew into a broader movement, drawing in labor unions and other activists who called out the rising cost of living and declining public services. On October 17th, an estimated 550,000 to 800,00 people protested nationwide.

Other countries began following suit. Since mid-September, demonstrations over high living costs, low wages, and lack of public services have broken out all across Europe. From Spain and Portugal to Germany and Albania, these protests have largely been led by Gen Z. In Spain and Portugal, protesters established encampments in public squares across major cities, demanding stronger laws to protect renters following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.

In Italy, the “Italia in Piazza”, or Italy in the Streets movement, brought thousands of protesters to the streets. Demonstrators called for better employment, healthcare, education, access to housing, and better wages. Major demonstrations have also taken place in Albania, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, and Serbia.

While the majority of demonstrations have been peaceful, some have escalated into riots involving looting, fires, and property destruction. Only 20% of the recorded events involved riots. However, the police response has been overwhelmingly severe, regardless of whether these protests have been peaceful or violent. French authorities have deployed military-style tactics to antagonize peaceful demonstrations, tactics that have long since drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors.

It is clear that all over the continent—all over the world— Gen Z is tired of waiting for promises to be delivered. They are demanding more than promises from political leaders. They want a future in which they can build secure lives. Young people are confronting economic and social challenges while remaining underrepresented in many of the institutions responsible for addressing them. Their participation in these movements shows that they are not willing to remain on the sidelines while decisions about their futures are made without them.

Across the world, communities are struggling to make rent, afford groceries, and childcare. We must demand more for ourselves, our communities and our future. And so, the fight for affordability continues.

author: Unknown
title: Varisheh Moradi: No policy of attrition can shake the foundations of our commitment
content:
Kurdish political prisoner Varisheh Moradi, who has been sentenced to death in Iran for the second time and is held in Evin Prison, wrote a letter on the occasion of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.


The letter penned by the Kurdish activist reads as follows:


“Systematic violence is an interconnected structure that begins within the home and extends into the public sphere. Yet, in its most blatant manifestation as state violence, it imposes itself through policies of elimination and denial, intimidation, censorship, repression, and detention, reaching its peak in execution. Meanwhile, through economic pressure, the shrinking of people’s means of subsistence, and under the shadow of war and its consequences, those in power have effectively placed a noose around the neck of society as a whole. Although the death sentence has been issued against me personally, this noose is tightening around everyone’s throat, casting the shadow of an imposed death over all of the society. I see the issuance of a death sentence for the second time as an attempt to turn time into an instrument of subjugation, replacing the “possibility of living” with the “anticipation of death.” Yet those in power fail to realize that the foundations of my commitment, and ours, to our historical and intellectual choices are so firmly established that no policy of attrition can shake them.


Against this backdrop, the shadow of war has significantly increased the number of suicides and killings of women across all regions of Iran. In a land whose historical memory is intertwined with narratives of goddesses and divine beings, how have we reached a point where women’s bodies and very existence have become objects of control, possession, and violation in the social sphere, while their independent will leads to their elimination in the political arena? Both have the same root: a patriarchal mentality sustained by the interconnected forces of power, hierarchy, and domination over women, which cannot tolerate the presence in politics of a woman who possesses her own will and has attained self-awareness. This system of thought fears women’s power and the truth of their existence because a conscious woman breaks free from the position of being possessed and objectified, questioning and challenging forms of authority and the foundations of domination.


For this reason, various labels are used to drive women out of social, political, and economic spheres. In politics, they call us “rebels” so that we may be sentenced to death, while in society, under the guise of tradition, they label crimes as “honor killings” to legitimize the same approach. Yet no force or system has the right to monopolize the power to define and name. By what standards and according to which moral values are these names and labels defined, and who has granted themselves such authority?


Nevertheless, the very fact that news of these crimes and femicides no longer remains hidden and shrouded in silence, as it once did, is itself a step forward and the result of years of struggle and perseverance. For years, attempts were made to portray violence against women as a private matter. But this violence is by no means a private matter. It always has psychological, physical, and structural dimensions and is not an individual problem but a collective one, a concern for society as a whole.


Confronting such a structure requires a continuous and comprehensive struggle against violence against women, one that extends from the home into the public sphere through breaking the silence, speaking out, criticizing and challenging mechanisms of domination, and seeking ways to resist them. This resistance is not the work of one individual or one woman, but the collective will and movement of all women.


For in the essence of “Woman, Life, Freedom,” “woman” is not a figure of submission and subordination, but the creative and liberating force of society. “Life,” in opposition to the culture of death and repression, means living with dignity and awareness. And “freedom” can only be achieved by dismantling every form of oppression and domination.


The struggle against violence against women is a defense of women themselves, a safeguarding of the meaning of life, and an opening of the path to freedom for society as a whole.


Jin, Jiyan, Azadî


Varisha Moradi – Women’s Ward, Evin Prison


November 25, 2026”
