author: Amy Goodman
title: National Book Award Winner Links Denial of US Visa to Palestine Advocacy
content:
Egyptian author and former political prisoner Abdelrahman ElGendy speaks about his new memoir, Huna.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an MFA in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.

“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells Democracy Now! about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”

We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet Mada Masr, whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.

“Mada carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in Mada Masr. “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

We are currently awaiting an Egyptian court decision on whether the closing of Mada Masr, the independent newspaper in Egypt, will stand. We’ll go to Cairo when we hear.

But right now we’re going to turn to what happened in the last few weeks here in this country, in New York, where we are. Novelists, essayists, poets and other writers from around the world took to the stage at the 77th annual National Book Awards ceremony in New York City last week. The winner of this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction, Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, though, was notably absent from the event, after the Trump administration denied his U.S. visa application, blocking him from entering the United States.

ElGendy’s debut book is called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, and chronicles his more than six years of imprisonment in Egypt following his arrest at the age of 17, alongside his father, during the crackdown on protests after the military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2013. He and his father were in their car, and Abdelrahman was taking a picture.

This is the moment the prize for nonfiction was presented by panel chair Robert Warrior.

ROBERT WARRIOR: It’s my distinct honor to announce that this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction goes to Abdelrahman ElGendy for Huna.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor, Helen Thomaides, then took the stage and read a statement written by ElGendy.

HELEN THOMAIDES: If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you. Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would one day end up in a book, that the guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist, that the slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how to render on the page the torture my body was enduring. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay …

author: Unknown
title: Rassemblement devant la prison des Baumettes dimanche 6 décembre
content:
Dimanche 6 décembre à 15h, rassemblons-nous devant la prison des Baumettes pour apporter notre soutien aux personnes enfermées !


Depuis la fin du mois de septembre, l'enthousiasme des lycéens à refuser l'état des choses est communicatif et nous a mis du baume au coeur. C'est cette joie et cette rage que l'État veut à tout prix empêcher de se répandre. Pour cela il réprime par tous les moyens : violences policières, interdictions de manifester, comparutions immédiates, couvre-feux et consignes explicites aux juges de distribuer des peines lourdes.


Des blocus aux manifestations, les mineur.es sont particulièrement visé.es. Iels subissent pressions et violences : mutilation et harcèlement par la police, traque et dénonciation par les proviseurs et chefs de services des foyers. Des conseils de discipline pleuvent et de nombreux·ses mineur.es passent devant le juge pour enfant.


De la rue à la prison, la justice donne à voir de manière criante son fonctionnement de classe et raciste. Comme le dit une proche d'un prisonnier des Baumettes “l'État se sert du mouvement social pour enfermer plus de pauvres et expulser plus d'arabes”. Pendant les comparutions immédiates, des peines de prison hyper dures ont été systématiquement assorties d'une ITF (Interdiction du Territoire Français) pour les personnes étrangères. Toujours la même politique raciste et sécuritaire : traquer, enfermer, expulser.


Suite aux nouvelles incarcérations, les galères des proches sont plus fortes que d'habitude : attente interminable pour obtenir un permis de visite, gros retards aux parloirs...La surpopulation des prisons atteint des records : des hamacs sont accrochés dans les cellules arrivants où s'entassent jusqu'à 4 personnes dans 9m². Les droits des prisonnier.es et de leurs proches, déjà peu respectés en temps normal, sont complètement bafoués.


Il y a de la résistance à l'intérieur, les prisonniers en promenade ont refusé massivement de rejoindre leurs cellules ces dernières semaines dans les prisons de Grenoble-Varces, de Toulouse-Seysses et de Lyon-Corbas.


Les élans de solidarité ont dépassé la rue avec des rassemblements devant les comicos et les tribunaux.


S'ils divisent pour mieux régner, notre solidarité dépasse les murs de leurs prisons.


Pour toutes ces raisons, il est important d'aller apporter notre soutien aux personnes incarcérées aux Baumettes :


Tous et toutes libres !

author: daniel
title: Solidarität mit den Gefangenen für den Frieden!
content:
Zum Internationalen Tag der Gefangenen für den Frieden am 1. Dezember bittet die War Resisters‘ International, zu deren Mitgliedern auch die Graswurzelrevolution als assoziierte Zeitschrift zählt, um Solidarität mit Menschen, die weltweit wegen ihrer Kriegsdienstverweigerung oder ihres Engagements für Frieden inhaftiert sind. Ihre Namen und Gefängnisadressen werden in der Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden veröffentlicht.

Die WRI ruft dazu auf, den Gefangenen Kartengrüße als Zeichen der Solidarität und der Ermutigung in die Haft zu schicken. Selbst wenn die Karten die Adressaten und Adressatinnen nicht erreichen sollten, machen sie deutlich, dass die Gefangenen nicht vergessen sind, was sich auf die Haftbedingungen günstig auswirken kann.

Die Liste enthält die Adressen von Gefangenen stellvertretend für viele andere, deren Adresse unbekannt ist oder die keine Publizität wünschen. Die Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden von 2025 ent­hielt Haft­adressen in Aser­baid­schan, Belarus, Eritrea, Sin­ga­pur, Südkorea, in der Ukraine und in den USA. Besonders katastrophal ist die Menschenrechtslage in Eritrea. Dort werden Männer und Frauen zu einem zeitlich unbegrenzten Nationaldienst gezwungen, teils Militär-, teils Arbeitsdienst unter härtesten Bedingungen. Die diesjährige Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden soll zum 1. Dezember 2026 auf www.wri-irg.org veröffentlicht werden.

Die Karten an die Gefangenen können sowohl gemeinsam und öffentlich als auch privat geschrieben werden. Die DFG-VK Mainz-Wiesbaden lädt ein zum gemeinsamen Schreiben der Karten an die Gefangenen für den Frieden mit Live-Musik von Strohfeuer Express, mit Film, Bilder-Schau, Speis und Trank: Zornheim bei Mainz, Samstag, 5. Dezember 2026, 13 Uhr, HerrBerts Kulturscheune, Untergasse 10, 55270 Zornheim. www.dfg-vk-mainz.de

Gernot Lennert (DFG-VK Mainz-Wiesbaden)

author: Unknown
title: Rivolte contadine ed emigrazione forzata
content:
Un approfondimento a cura del

Collettivo Politico Addunati

 in merito alle mobilitazioni degli agricoltori odierne con uno sguardo che parte da un’analisi storica delle più importanti rivolte nel mondo agricolo della regione calabrese.


Le lotte agrarie in Calabria nel secondo dopoguerra e le radici dello spopolamento


Siamo alla fine di agosto, il mese dello stacco. Il lavoro — quel mostro multiforme che impone regole fisse e schematizza le nostre giornate — sembra concedere quasi a tutti una pausa dal giogo della produzione continua. Le temperature sono elevatissime, le giornate si scandiscono al ritmo delle alette dei condizionatori: un su e giù continuo seguito dal nostro sguardo fisso. Si potrebbe scappare, cercare un po’ di pace fuori dalle proprie case. Inutile dire che, provandoci, si resterebbe delusi. Strade, spiagge, montagne, colline e pianure: tutto è affollato. Turismo di massa, prezzi alle stelle e stress. Nulla che ricordi vagamente la possibilità di staccare la spina. Pare che il tentativo di trasformare ogni luogo abitabile in un centro commerciale itinerante stia finalmente funzionando. Ogni casa è una vetrina; ogni angolo vuoto tra i vicoli dei centri storici o lungo gli stradoni di provincia diventa buono per piazzare tavoli e sedie. Bar, ristoranti, lidi, camioncini di cibo da consumare in fretta. Il paradigma del «potremmo campare solo di turismo» si materializza davanti ai nostri occhi. L’illusione che basti sfruttare il patrimonio materiale (paesaggi, borghi arroccati, città) e immateriale (cultura culinaria, dialetti, folklore) per vivere di rendita è ormai diventata realtà. Del resto, è la stessa industria culturale e dell’intrattenimento — tra televisione, social network e piattaforme di streaming — a far passare l’idea che in Italia, nel 2026, non abbia senso investire tempo, fatica e denaro in nulla che non riguardi la ristorazione e l’accoglienza. Tra foodblogger, video-ricette e programmi come MasterChef, 4 Ristoranti o 4 Hotel, ci si convince dell’inevitabilità di un declino che appare irrecuperabile. Nel frattempo, assistiamo ogni giorno allo smantellamento del tessuto produttivo del Paese: delocalizzazione industriale, assenza di qualsiasi piano di rinnovamento, abbandono delle terre o svendita di piccoli appezzamenti divenuti insostenibili per costi di produzione e dispendio di forza-lavoro rispetto al ricavo netto.


La retorica bucolica e la realtà dei campi


Ma agosto volge al termine. Agosto finisce e tocca trovare un lavoro. Dalle nostre parti, questo è il tempo della vendemmia — o almeno lo era. Conosciamo bene le retoriche spicciole e false che accompagnano l’agricoltura. Il senso comune — quello di chi non ha mai messo piede in campagna se non per un’«aperivigna» — associa il lavoro agricolo a un’esistenza bucolica, a un idilliaco ritorno alla natura. È la solita poeticizzazione della vita campestre. La realtà è ben diversa: ore sotto il sole, raccolti altalenanti, condizioni spesso inumane e l’assenza pressoché totale di tutele statali. Basta una grandinata, un virus delle piante o un parassita sconosciuto per azzerare il lavoro di anni. A queste variabili — solo in apparenza “casuali”, perché cambiamento climatico e riscaldamento globale sono tutt’altro che fatalità, checché ne dica un noto Ministro che liquida la questione sostenendo che «d’estate fa caldo e d’inverno fa freddo» — si sommano le crisi strutturali. Dal crollo finanziario del 2008 fino all’economia di guerra permanente a cui i governi cercano di abituarci, l’aumento del costo del carburante e il crollo dei prezzi alla produzione hanno reso il lavoro della terra insostenibile per i piccoli coltivatori. La Calabria, segnata da una storica fragilità economica, subisce tutto questo con un peso doppio. Eppure, nel torpore generale, gli agricoltori calabresi hanno deciso di alzare la testa e scendere in piazza per pretendere misure reali di sostegno. Non è la prima volta che contadini e coltivatori diretti si mobilitano contro l’abbandono delle istituzioni per rivendicare dignità e riconoscimento. Ripercorrere alcune delle principali proteste avvenute nella regione tra il 1947 e il 1957 aiuta a illuminare il legame diretto tra lo smantellamento sistematico dell’agricoltura calabrese e l’emigrazione forzata.


1947-1957: un decennio di lotte e repressione

author: Rudi Hartono, Peter Boyle
title: ‘Rising authoritarianism and militarism’ in Indonesia under Prabowo
content:
As the Indonesian economy sinks deeper into crisis, President Prabowo Subianto's government is becoming more authoritarian. Peter Boyle spoke to Rudi Hartono, one of the founding editors of the progressive publication Merdika.id about the current political situation. Hartono, a former editor of Berdikari Online left the People’s Democratic Party (PRD) because it moved to the right.

Recent events in Indonesia — the deployment of thousands of soldiers and tanks in Jakarta following reports of electronic surveillance [wiretapping] targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other government officials and the police raid on Gadjah Mada University — are reminiscent of the Suharto dictatorship’s New Order regime. Is a new and dangerous situation developing? If so, what lies behind it?

Yes, we are witnessing clear symptoms of rising authoritarianism and militarism. Although many had predicted this trajectory since Prabowo’s election victory, the speed and intensity of the process have been striking.

Since June 2026, the military has once again been deployed to confront protests — a move that evokes memories of the New Order. Large-scale troop mobilisations occurred during the demonstrations on October 20 (marking two years of the Prabowo-Gibran administration) and October 28 (Youth Pledge Day).

On one of those days, I received a WhatsApp message containing a video of tanks and marching soldiers on the streets, accompanied by the caption: “Thank your friends [referring to former PRD members who now support Prabowo and hold positions in government] for bringing the military back onto the streets.”

Yet the presence of soldiers on the streets only completes the picture of authoritarian consolidation that has taken shape over the past two years under Prabowo-Gibran.

Today, the 1998 reformasi has become little more than an artifact. Political power is once again concentrated in the executive (the presidency).

Many of the president’s remarks in speeches have quickly turned into policy — such as the roof-tile standardisation program or foreign-language lessons. The House of Representatives (DPR) has been reduced to a chorus, much like under the New Order.

There is no genuine opposition in the DPR. Even the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDIP), which remains outside the ruling coalition, has tended to be permissive toward the deteriorating situation.

The judiciary has suffered a similar fate: it is filled with government-aligned figures. The mechanisms of checks and balances have effectively disappeared.

It is not only the legislative and judicial branches that have been subdued. We are also seeing a process of recentralisation that is stripping regional and local governments of authority, fiscal resources, and responsibilities. Regional autonomy — one of the key achievements of the 1998 reform — is now little more than a skeleton being dragged toward its grave.

At the same time, freedom of expression is being heavily repressed. Paid "buzzers" [opinion-shapers] are deployed to drown out public criticism on social media, while the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs actively removes critical content. Cases of threats, intimidation, and doxxing against citizens in digital spaces are common. Mainstream media have adopted self-censorship. Under former President Joko Widowo (Jokowi), certain individuals monitored the media from the outside; under Prabowo, his people have entered the newsrooms themselves to supervise from within.

The presidential wiretapping issue, which provided the pretext for mobilising more than 20,000 troops and tanks on Jakarta’s streets, cannot be read simply as a clash between two elite factions. It more closely resembles the autogolpe [“self-coup”] schemes frequently seen in Latin America.

In my view, the issue was manufactured to serve three purposes at once. First, it supplied a justification for deploying more soldiers onto the streets. Second, it diverted public attention from structural problems — economic crisis, corruption, militarism, and others — toward a security narrative. Third, it was a crude tactic to redirect vertical public anger at the regime into a drama of elite infighting.

Before the wiretapping story surfaced, the regime was already under pressure from multiple fronts: forest fires in Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua; mass food poisoning from the free nutritious meal program (MBG) that has affected more than 50,000 children; the militarisation and expanding role …

author: Darius Tahir
title: Health Tech Is Pushing Data-Collecting “Smart” Implants That Raise Cost of Care
content:
Doctors can charge for examining data collected by devices that have little evidence for benefiting patient health.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said.

Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’”

It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer.

Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit, Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t.

Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues.

Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment.

The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court.

Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.”

Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future.

“The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.”

The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “the world’s first and only” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices — from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors — that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance.

However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes.

There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data — is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect.

Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries …

author: Unknown
title: Narges Mohammadi calls for the protection of women against cyber threats
content:
Women in Iran face legal and societal threats. While women's rights organisations continue to call for the strengthening and enforcement of existing laws and institutions that safeguard women's dignity and security, Nobel Peace Prize-winning activist Narges Mohammadi has released a video message.


In her message, shared on a digital platform, Narges Mohammadi called for solidarity with and support for women who are subjected to organised cyber threats and interference because of their activities in social, political, media and human rights fields.


Narges Mohammadi said that, in recent years, she herself has faced harassment, insults, death threats and widespread gender-based cyber violence, adding that these attacks continued even while she was imprisoned.


Addressing the methods of cyber harassment targeting women, Narges Mohammadi explained that these attacks include organised smear campaigns, the exposure of personal information, insults, misogyny, the spread of misinformation and the circulation of fabricated images generated using artificial intelligence (AI). She emphasised that the aim of these attacks is to isolate, intimidate and silence women.


Drawing attention to statistics, Narges Mohammadi said that more than 70 percent of women journalists, activists and those in leadership positions experience cyber harassment. She warned that such attacks must not silence women or force them to withdraw from public life.


At the end of her statement, Narges Mohammadi reiterated the need for solidarity and collective support to protect women facing smear campaigns and cyber threats.

author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 19 November 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Making sense of the Digital Fairness Act, a very unmerry birthday to the Digital Omnibus, and more!

Last week, the European Commission put digital fairness on the menu with a proposal for its long-awaited Digital Fairness Act (DFA) – and we have some food for thought.

This law will strengthen consumer protection against manipulative and exploitative commercial practices, such as fake notifications designed to keep bringing us back to an app, endless scrolling that keeps us online way longer than you intended, and other personalised techniques used by online services that exploit our vulnerabilities. First things first, proposal actually takes some important steps forward by introducing new prohibitions on deceptive design, extending specific protections beyond the biggest online platforms, and recognising the harms associated with addictive digital features. However, we were left wondering – why promise digital fairness yet leave the users to do all the work instead of holding manipulative online services responsible? Read our analysis on Tech Policy Press.

Despite it all, the DFA proposal – something that actually might protect our rights online – is a welcome respite in the current wave of deregulation in the EU. This week, we’re also reckoning with the fact that November 19, 2026 marks one year since the Commission published the proposals for the Digital Omnibus. We, along with many other civil society organisations, had warned that this would be a massive reopening of EU’s core digital protections that would risk dismantling the very foundation of human rights and tech policy in the EU. One year on, it seems like we were granted Apollo’s gift of prophecy. On this unfortunate occasion, we’re standing strong with 100 organisations, experts, academics and more to urge EU lawmakers to not simplify away our rights.

In this edition, you can also explore our extremely thorough guide to the European Parliament’s 1840 amendments to the Digital Omnibus on Data, focusing on what they would mean for privacy, data protection and, ultimately, people’s rights. Yes, 1840, you read that right. Hungry for more? Also read our thoughts on the EU governments’ position on the Digital Omnibus.

1,840 amendments, one basic question: will the Data Omnibus simplify EU digital rules or weaken people’s rights? author: By Jo Kimmy, Contributor
title: From Hospitals to Palantir HQ: Protests Across England Over Controversial Healthcare Data Deal
content:
London, England — “We need to take our power back! Our UK government needs to represent the interests of the British public, who elected them into power, not the Zionist entity,” said Taby Khan, a health research scientist protesting outside The Royal London Hospital.


On October 1, doctors, nurses, health care workers and members of the public took to the streets at more than 40 locations across England, demanding an end to the controversial £330 million ($442 million) contract between the National Health Service (NHS) and U.S. technology company Palantir.


The mobilization was organized by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Health Workers for a Free Palestine, Amnesty International, Medact, Keep Our NHS Public, and other groups. They argue that a company known for its work with military and immigration agencies, including the development of AI and surveillance technologies, should not have access to the sensitive health data of

60 million people

 in England.


The protests began outside hospitals across the country, including four locations in London, before culminating in a demonstration outside Palantir’s London headquarters.


Located in central London, Palantir’s London office is the company’s

largest globally

, employing more people than its Silicon Valley headquarters. In front of the building, with its dark, heavily tinted windows and no visible signs identifying it as Palantir’s offices, hundreds of people chanted, held signs and displayed a giant symbolic notice calling for the contract to be terminated.


The demo was largely peaceful, although verbal tensions arose between anti-Palantir protesters and Zionist agitators who were trying to disrupt the demonstration and provoke tensions. Some protesters accused the police of allowing these tensions to develop.


The protest brought together concerns that might otherwise remain separate: the privatization of public services, the security of patient information, the expansion of surveillance technology and Palantir’s involvement in war crimes.


Palantir and the NHS: Who Owns Britain’s Health Data?


The NHS was officially

established

 on July 5, 1948, marking the first time a Western country provided free medical care to its entire population, regardless of status.


The relationship between the NHS and the U.S. tech company

began with an “emergency” contract

 under which Palantir offered to support the vaccination program and data management projects. In 2023, with little consideration for alternative solutions, Palantir was awarded the

contract

 to deliver the

NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP)

.


As the

NHS Data Professionals

 explain: “duplications and local variations prevent smooth linkage across datasets and regions.” The FDP is intended to help NHS organizations connect information held across different systems, making it easier to coordinate services, plan capacity and support operational decisions.


The underlying challenge is real: information can be fragmented across hospitals, general practices and regional services, making it difficult to build a joined-up picture of patient care.


Data analysts have raised concerns about the FDP’s highly centralized structure. Palantir supplies data engineers and manages the underlying infrastructure, which provides limited transparency and leaves NHS organizations with less ability to independently adapt the software to their needs.


From Military Intelligence to Public Healthcare


“Palantir is here to disrupt…and, when it’s necessary, to scare our enemies and, on

occasion, kill them.” –

Alex Karp, Palantir CEO


During the protest in front of Palantir’s London headquarters, a letter written by an anonymous NHS data analyst was read aloud. In it, the analyst described how she had begun to hate her job, working with software developed by a company responsible for the deaths of hundreds of her healthcare colleagues.


Palantir initially focused on government, military and intelligence agencies before expanding into the commercial and wider public sectors. The NHS FDP operates on the Foundry software, which is marketed as a system for the “modern enterprise.” Its other products include Gotham, used for “defense and resilience,” and Apollo, which manages software deployment.


The company’s military business is central to why many healthcare workers oppose its role in the NHS. Its

close involvement in U.S. and Israeli military operations

, alongside accusations of complicity in war …

title: Giorgio Agamben: The death of the word?
content:
Michelangelo,

Cumaean Sibyl

 (c. 1511), Sistine Chapel, Vatican City


This short article was originally published under the title “Morte della parola?” in the Italian newspaper

Paese Sera

 on 8 February 1968. It has been republished in the latest issue of the French magazine

Entétement

, although the original version can be found on the

La Voce di Fiore

 archive website. A Spanish translation of the same can be found at th magazine

Ficción de la razón

.


A book has recently been published in Paris,

Of Grammatology

 (1967), a work destined to cause a stir not only in the field of linguistic studies. Jacques Derrida, one of the most original figures in the new wave of French philosophical criticism, begins with the observation that, today, “through a movement whose necessity we can barely glimpse, everything that, for at least twenty centuries, has tended to be defined under the name of language, is beginning to be summarised under the name of writing”. It does indeed seem that writing—which, according to Rousseau, was nothing more than a complement to speech—is gradually freeing itself from its subordination to the phonetic medium, to the point of reversing its traditional relationship with language: writing would therefore not be a technique in the service of language, but rather, on the contrary, it is language that can be considered a specific case, an aspect, of writing.


To better understand the phenomenon to which Derrida refers when he speaks of writing dissociated from the phonetic element, one need only consider the example of mathematics, whose symbolic notation does not refer to any spoken language. If we consider that today we are witnessing a process of mathematisation across all the sciences, the “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon (readers who have followed recent news regarding the

in vitro

 synthesis of living matter, carried out by certain American scientists, will recall having heard talk of writing and “programmes” even in relation to the most elementary processes of the living cell). The “liberation” of writing described by Derrida becomes an extremely concrete phenomenon.


On the basis of these premises, Derrida deduces the need for a pure science of writing, which considers writing prior to speech and independently of it: this science is, precisely, “grammatology”; and, to define its aims, it suffices to substitute this term for “semiology”, the term Saussure uses to outline the programme of his famous

Course in General Linguistics

: “We shall call it grammatology… and, as it does not yet exist, we cannot say what it will be; but it has a right to exist, and its place is determined in advance”. The age of speech, which began under the creative power of the verb, is drawing to a close before our very eyes; the character of this new age might be summed up in the following formula: “In the beginning was the written word’’.


Whilst it is true that, from this perspective, linguistics must become a mere branch of grammatology, Derrida seems, however, to overlook the fact that a science already exists which considers language not as speech, but as code and writing; consequently, grammatology itself should necessarily be understood as a sub-branch or a section of that science. This is cybernetics, which, from its beginnings in Wiener’s theories, defined its world as a universe of writing and coding. The very idea of grammatology is already fully contained within the notion of “programme”, one of the key concepts of cybernetics. Etymologically, “programme” —pro-grammer— means “to put the letter (that is,

writing

) first”, whilst “prophecy” means, by contrast, “to put the word first”. Indeed, in the programme assigned to an electronic brain, everything that constitutes the living, phonetic element of language is erased to make way for a system of absolute writing that can be deciphered but not pronounced. It is fair to say that, up to now, our civilisation has known two types of language that have gradually diverged: the language of science is, essentially, written language —code, writing—, whilst the language of poetry and philosophical thought is spoken language —breath, word—. Nevertheless, these two domains—which, for convenience’s sake, we might call the “sphere of the programme” and the “sphere of prophecy”—are drawing ever closer together today thanks to cybernetics; through the mathematisation of human phenomena, cybernetics …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Harassment won’t stop a son’s search for his missing father
content:
Marklen Lariosa, son of missing Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) labor organizer William Lariosa, speaks during a rally in Davao City on the first anniversary of his father’s disappearance on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kath Cortez/Davao Today

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through.”

Is it a mistake for a son to demand justice and accountability?

Marklen, son of disappeared labor organizer William Lariosa, raised this question following the recent incident of harassment and surveillance he experienced. Members of his family were alarmed after two unidentified individuals were looking for his residence on the night of October 25.

He told Bulatlat that this was the first time such an event had happened since his father, a labor organizer under Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) Southern Mindanao, was abducted in Quezon, Bukidnon, on April 10, 2024.

Marklen could not think of other possible reasons, suspecting that the incident may have something to do with his continuing involvement in campaigns and mobilizations that demand the surfacing of Lariosa. “Is it a mistake for a son to search for his missing father?” he further asked.

Read: After 2 years, son laments continuing disappearance of Mindanao labor organizer

Neighbors of the Lariosa family in their hometown in Davao de Oro province were the ones who encountered the two individuals. They reportedly wore helmets and were on board a black motorcycle, introducing themselves as “collectors” when they were asked.

For Marklen, the response and presence of the two raised suspicions. Aside from the fact that they visited the community around 7 p.m., which is outside the regular working hours, Marklen said that he did not apply for any financial loan.

After the incident, he was concerned for the safety of his family, prompting them to lodge a blotter report with the barangay. However, he stood firm that it won’t stop him from continuing his cause.

Desaparecidos, an organization of families and friends of enforced disappearance victims, denounced the incident, urging the government to put an end to this kind of harassment.

“Family members searching for their disappeared loved ones have to endure threats and harassment from state forces on top of the terrible uncertainty and emotional turmoil they are already going through,” JL Burgos, Desaparecidos chairperson, said in a statement.

Rights groups Karapatan and the Center for Trade Union and Human Rights (CTUHR) also expressed strong condemnations about what happened.

Marklen, a member of the National Board of Desaparecidos, has raised a possibility that the two individuals who recently visited their neighborhood might be connected to those who visited their house several times prior to the disappearance of his father.

He said they were visited by individuals who allegedly introduced themselves as state agents once in 2022 and three times in 2023, accusing Lariosa of being involved in communist insurgency. There were warnings, he added, that they would get dragged into it if they would not cooperate.

The series of visits was reportedly the primary reason why Lariosa was forced to take refuge in Bukidnon. Marklen affirmed that his father, who remains missing, had been a labor organizer.

On July 8, the Supreme Court required certain commanders and elements of Philippine Army units to comment on the petition for review on certiorari filed by the family.

Read: Military ordered to reply to missing Mindanao labor organizer’s case

Since 2024, KMU Southern Mindanao has documented 57 cases of human rights violations against its members and organizers.

The labor group released a statement on October 24, presenting the faces of some individuals, including former high-ranking New People’s Army (NPA) member Roberto Rosete Jr., who allegedly harassed KMU’s leaders and members.

Read: Groups decry surveillance of KMU office in Southern Mindanao

Marklen called for an end to any form of harassment and intimidation against families of the disappeared, pointing out that achieving justice is their only goal. (RVO)

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Peasant organizer persists despite surveillance
content:
Jesus Monasterial. (Photo from Photo from Tanggol Magsasaka-TK)

Repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety.

When he was a university student, he questioned the purpose of agricultural education. Now he is organizing landless farmers and fisherfolk.

Jesus Monasterial has spent more than two years working with rural communities in Southern Tagalog. However, his work resulted in repeated surveillance by state forces, peasant groups said.

On October 31, Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan reported that a police intelligence operative identified as “Bruno” had been asking about Monasterial’s whereabouts in Lian, Batangas. The operative was reportedly previously assigned in Nasugbu.

At the time, Monasterial was assisting a protest camp in Barangay San Diego, where farmers, fisherfolk, and residents opposed the possible demolition of several houses.

“I was on my way back to the people’s protest camp in San Diego when news reached us that someone had been asking about my personal information,” he said.

The camp was established by Samahang Mangangawil 1979 and the San Diego Homeowners’ Association, with support from the Katipunan ng mga Samahang Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) and Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas–Timog Katagalugan (PAMALAKAYA-TK).

The incident prompted fellow organizers to discuss security measures. They also plan to file a complaint before the Commission on Human Rights (CHR).

Monasterial’s involvement in peasant organizing began at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) where he was enrolled in BS Agricultural Biotechnology.

Coming from a family of farmers in Bicol, where his grandparents worked as agricultural tenants, he became increasingly critical of an agricultural education system that he said served the interests of transnational corporations rather than addressing farmers’ lack of land and government support.

Through the League of Filipino Students–UPLB, he became involved in social issues action and joined community immersions with farmers in Tartaria, Silang, Cavite, as well as Mangyan communities in Mindoro and Dumagat communities in Rizal.

These experiences led him to leave his studies and become a full-time organizer. He now serves as deputy secretary-general of KASAMA-TK.

His work involves staying in communities, conducting consultations and political education, and helping establish local farmers and fisherfolk associations.

“Being a full-time organizer means devoting my entire time to the communities and being far from my loved ones,” he said, adding that he had to set aside his plan to finish college.

The October 31 incident was not the first reported surveillance involving Monasterial.

On July 19, 2026, soldiers from the 16th Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army reportedly sought to identify the organizers of KASAMA-TK’s Regional Peasant Consultation in Barangay Malinis, Lemery, Batangas.

On September 21, a man introducing himself as “Del” Dela Cruz reportedly approached a member of Sugarfolks’ Unity for Genuine Agricultural Reform (SUGAR-Batangas), attempting to persuade the member to leave the organization and provide information about its activities.

According to Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan, the man showed footage of a protest outside the Department of Agriculture regional office led by the Alyansa ng Magsasaka para sa Kumpensasyon (AMK), SUGAR-Batangas, KAISAHAN, and KASAMA-TK. He allegedly warned the member against working with Monasterial, claiming that the organizer was “already drawing attention.”

The protest resulted in a dialogue with government representatives to demand agricultural inputs and implements for farmers and farmworkers affected by successive calamities.

The groups also cited previous incidents in Barangay Casile, Laguna; Lupang Ramos and Tartaria, Cavite; and Coron, Palawan.

Monasterial said that the repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety. “Repeated surveillance limits my movements as an organizer and makes me fear returning home to my family because they might also be targeted by the state due to my advocacy.”

Despite the threats, Monasterial said that his work remains rooted in the struggles of farmers and farmworkers.

title: Kurdistan Regional Government: We reject the use of military rhetoric and threats
content:
Kurdistan Region’s Prime Minister Masrour Barzani chaired the KRG Council of Ministers’ meeting today. The meeting focused primarily on the KRG’s position regarding measures taken yesterday by the federal government of Iraq.


The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region is committed to fulfilling all its constitutional obligations and demands the full provision of its constitutional rights: “The KRG has consistently expressed its readiness to resolve outstanding issues with the federal government within the framework of the Constitution. Consequently, the KRG expresses its deep concern and strong protest regarding the statement issued on behalf of the spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, which violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region. This statement is a dangerous indication of a lack of belief in the federal system and represents an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime, which contradicts the Iraqi Constitution. The KRG rejects the use of military rhetoric and threats, which appear to stem from a premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.”


The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region has consistently supported measures to combat corruption and illegal activities, and has cooperated and coordinated with the federal government and will continue to do so to eliminate illicit practices. It called for the comprehensive eradication of corruption and oil smuggling across all of Iraq.


The Council of Ministers stressed that the Kurdistan Region is the product of the sacrifices of the heroic Peshmerga and thousands of martyrs; it is not a gift bestowed upon the people of Kurdistan: “The Kurdistan Region has played an active and influential role in establishing the current federal system in Iraq, regards itself as a co-owner of that system, and will never relinquish its constitutional rights, which extend far beyond salaries, budgets, and financial entitlements. They also encompass political rights and the legitimate cause of the people of Kurdistan.”


The KRG Council of Ministers stressed that issues between the Kurdistan Region and the federal government must be resolved through dialogue, negotiations, and mutual understanding within the constitutional framework, calling for the full implementation of the permanent Iraqi Constitution.


“The primary reason these issues remain unresolved is the failure to implement the Constitution, particularly Article 140, which has been neglected for years, with no steps taken to normalize the situation in the disputed Kurdish territories. In accordance with the Constitution, the Federal Council of Iraq should be established, and the Federal Supreme Court reconstituted on a constitutional basis that reflects all components of Iraq.”


The Council of Ministers expressed its gratitude to the Kurdistani people, as well as to all political parties, forces, and components, urging them to maintain their national stance, unity, and solidarity in defense of the constitutional rights of the people of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Region's constitutional framework. It also called upon the Kurdistan Region's representatives in the Iraqi Parliament and the federal government to continue their national role in defending the rights of the Kurdistani people.


The Council of Ministers reaffirmed its support for freedom of opinion and expression. However, it emphasized that anyone who acts against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region, constitutional principles, or Kurdistan’s national interests and incites people to create chaos and oppose the rights of the Kurdistani people should face appropriate legal action.

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Trump Judicial Nominee at Center of GOP Drama Signed Off on Deadly Boat Strikes
content:
Nominated to be a federal judge, T. Elliot Gaiser signed off on deadly airstrikes experts call extrajudicial executions.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Media coverage of Republican infighting over judicial nominee T. Elliot Gaiser has focused on the strong words exchanged between Texas Senators John Cornyn and Ted Cruz. President Donald Trump nominated Gaiser to become a federal judge in Texas, but Cornyn blocked a crucial committee vote on November 18 to advance the pick forward.

“Everyone knows that I am a notorious cusser and screamer and that Ted is a fragile thing,” Cornyn said on November 21 in a social media post describing a previous heated exchange between the two lawmakers. Cornyn has argued that Gaiser is not from Texas and has little trial experience, while Cruz accuses Cornyn of handing an open judicial seat to Democrats.

However, what has received far less attention is Gaiser’s role in producing the legal opinion that greenlit the U.S. military’s deadly airstrikes on civilian boats in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean that the Trump administration has accused, without evidence, of smuggling drugs. The strikes have killed more than 200 people in what human rights groups say are effectively extrajudicial executions in blatant violation of U.S. and international law.

“We’re talking about legal opinions used to justify military strikes that have killed hundreds of people, alongside a broader pattern of putting the president’s personal interests ahead of the law,” said Michael Teter, co-founder of the Legal Accountability Center, in a statement.

Gaiser currently serves as assistant attorney general in the Justice Department, where he leads the Office of Legal Counsel (OLC). He is also Trump’s nominee for a lifetime federal judgeship in the Northern District of Texas. Cornyn used a procedural maneuver last week to block the Senate Judiciary Committee from advancing Gaiser’s nomination. However, Cornyn remains under pressure from Cruz and other conservatives to reverse course and allow a vote on Gaiser as Republicans race to confirm Trump nominees before a Democratic majority takes over in January.

Meanwhile, the Legal Accountability Center filed a bar complaint against Gaiser on November 18, calling for an investigation into his role in providing legal cover for the deadly airstrikes on civilian boats in international waters. The complaint also cites a series of opinions released by the OLC that allegedly prioritize Trump’s personal interests over federal law, including a controversial opinion declaring that the Presidential Records Act, a key oversight law, is unconstitutional and does not apply to Trump.

“Government lawyers have a duty to tell the president when the law says ‘no,’ not simply find ways to justify whatever he wants to do,” Teter said, adding that the allegations are “extraordinarily serious.”

At the center of the complaint is a secret legal opinion written under Gaiser’s leadership to provide legal justification for the Trump administration’s airstrikes on civilian boats suspected of smuggling drugs. Issued on September 5, 2025, the legal opinion followed an infamous September 2 attack in which two shipwrecked survivors of an initial U.S. airstrike were killed by a secondary (or “double tap”) strike while clinging to the wreckage in the water.

Rep. Jim Himes (D-Connecticut), who serves on the House Intelligence Committee and saw video of the strikes, pointed out that the second strike was impermissible by U.S. military manual standards. The bar complaint against Gaiser alleges he failed to exercise independent judgment and provided legal cover for unlawful killings.

While the legal opinion remains classified, court filings indicate the 49-page memo was signed by Gaiser, according to the bar complaint. Members of Congress who have seen the memo have publicly outlined its legal reasoning, which rests on a theory that the U.S. is engaged in a formal armed conflict with drug smugglers. The Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA), a human rights group, calls this reasoning “badly flawed.”

author: Harriet Williamson
title: US Military Set to Detonate Toxic Lead Bomb in Iowa
content:
Children, pregnant women and chronically ill people in Iowa are being advised to evacuate as the US army prepares to blow up a stockpile of munitions laced with lead on Wednesday. 


Nearly five tonnes of unstable bomb-making chemicals stored at a base in Middletown, Iowa, are scheduled for detonation despite serious risks to human health. 


The detonation is expected to send a toxic plume of lead-containing dust particles over eastern Iowa and into the neighbouring state of Illinois, where toxins will likely settle on farmland, homes and playgrounds. 


There is no safe level of exposure to lead, which is a neurotoxin. 


350 farms could be exposed

 to the toxic lead dust, according to the US Department of Agriculture. 


Children and pregnant women are particularly at risk as exposure to lead can interfere with fetal brain development, cause cognitive damage and increase the likelihood of miscarriages and premature births. 


In adults, lead exposure is linked to decreased kidney function, fertility issues and heart problems, along with

 increased risks

 of various cancers.


Iowa has the

second-highest rate of cancer

 among US states, and is one of only three states where rates of cancer are rising. 


A lawsuit was filed by environmental groups to block the detonation, but the US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Monday that it could go ahead.


Journalist Abby Martin called it “an emergency of [the US army’s] own making because of their own negligence and disregard”. 


She told

 BreakThrough News on Tuesday

: “I just can’t wrap my mind around the fact that an industry that has a budget of over $1tn cannot incorporate a safe disposal mechanism for these toxic chemicals it is constantly manufacturing.


“I think at the end of the day, they just know they can override local governments.”


Federal officials say the detonation is needed because the degraded material could explode on its own. 


The US army initially contracted a company to chemically neutralise the weapons after it became aware of the degrading cache at a military base in March,

the New York Times reported

. However, it cancelled the deal just two months later and decided to blow up the munitions instead. 


Environmental

assessment documents

 from the US military state that while the chemical route for disposal “offered environmental protections by avoiding a blast plume, it was eliminated from detailed study due to unacceptable risk to human safety”. This was because the process required more “hands-on” handling by workers over long days.


The Department of Health and Human Services (HSS) told pregnant women, children and those with chronic illnesses

to evacuate on Tuesday

, with HHS principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response saying “you definitely want to be out of that area”.


The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown makes medium and large calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.

author: Kodao Productions
title: NPA-Mindoro reports failed AFP attack, 4 gov’t casualties
content:
The New People’s Army (NPA) reported the death of four government troopers in a clash at Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro on Monday, thwarting a 1

st

 Infantry Battalion-Philippine Army strike operation.


The NPA said a unit of its Lucio de Guzman Command successfully defended itself against the raid at its temporary encampment in Sitio Gatol, Barangay San Roque, withdrawing safely after the firefight.


An ABS-CBN report of the incident quoted 203rd Infantry Brigade-Philippine Army commander Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo claiming only two soldiers were wounded and are at a stable condition at a hospital. The report also stated that said the clash started at around 8:35 AM.


The NPA, however, said civilians who were at the scene after the encounter reported that four soldiers were killed. The Red army likewise refuted 1st IB’s claim that firearms and equipment were seized from the guerillas.


The NPA added that its fighters spotted the approaching soldiers and opened fire on them before they could reach the camp.NPA-Mindoro spokesperson Madaay Gasic said their latest victory against the Armed Forces of the Philippines demonstrate the Red army’s will to fight and the people’s “unwavering support.” Gasic also belied Ragudo’s claim civilians tipped off the miitary about the NPA’s presence in the area.


“The people of Bulalacao and all the people of Mindoro celebrate the heroic resistance of their army against the enemy,” Gasic said. #

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Women seek justice for Duterte drug war victims
content:
Photo by Jonathan Sta. Rosa/NCCP

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Seeing her son crying as she was about to leave for the market, she gave him a piece of candy. She later found him dead upon coming back home.

Emily Soriano was among the women whose loved ones were killed during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. They shared their accounts of the killings, highlighting their continuing struggle for justice with leaders of the World Council of Churches (WCC).

Members of Rise Up for Life and for Rights, a network of relatives of people killed during the anti-drug campaign, recounted their experiences during a dialogue organized by the National Council of Churches in the Philippines (NCCP).

The dialogue formed part of Thursdays in Black, a WCC campaign that seeks to end violence against women.

Aside from Soriano, Normita Lopez recounted how police shot her son despite his attempt to surrender. According to her, witnesses saw him raise both hands and plead with the police not to shoot but an officer pushed him down and shot him four times in the body and once in his right hand.

For her part, Jane Lee said that people ignored their pleas for justice before the WCC facilitated her travel to bring the families’ stories to the United Nations.

Estrella Nonay said, “I didn’t know how to get justice, so I joined Rise Up because I believe that if one of us gets justice, it is also justice for my son.”

“We are sharing with you sacred stories. Now that you have heard them, you are witnesses. We invite the WCC to stand in solidarity with the families of the victims in their quest for justice,” Deaconess Norma Dollaga of Rise Up said.

Rev. Merlyn Hyde Riley, vice-moderator of the WCC Central Committee, said that the testimonies exposed deeper structural, political, economic, social, and spiritual issues behind the killings. “No human being deserves to be treated in the ways you have described your loved ones having been treated,” Hyde Riley said.

Rev. Dr. Karen Georgia Thompson, general minister and president of the United Church of Christ and president of the World Communion of Reformed Churches, also called on churches to confront state violence against poor and marginalized communities.

She said that poor and marginalized communities bear the brunt of programs designed to harm them and urged churches to uphold human rights and dignity. (DAA)

title: Torino: sesto weekend di fila di mobilitazione contro il carovita di guerra!
content:
Ripubblichiamo il comunicato di

Torino contro il riarmo

 sulla giornata di sciopero generale.


Torino è stata attraversata da una giornata di sciopero generale che ha portato in piazza almeno 50 mila persone, di cui 20 mila nello spezzone sociale, formato da: studenti medi, universitari, lavoratori, sindacati di base, comitati di insegnanti, gruppi autonomi di lavoratori,comitati contro i data center e ambientalisti. 


Alle 9 e 30 piazza XVIII dicembre era gremita di persone e il corteo, per riuscire a partire tanti erano i manifestanti, ha dovuto aspettare fino alle 11 per riuscire a muoversi. 


L’entusiasmo di una giornata di sciopero generale si è respirato fin dal primo momento, in molti hanno pensato allo sciopero del 3 ottobre del 2025, in molti hanno iniziano piacevolmente ad abituarsi, che si può scendere in strada in tanti e bloccare davvero la metropoli. 


Per raggiungere la piazza ci sono stati almeno una decina di pre concentramenti fra scuole, università e quartieri, ed un altro corteo studentesco, con la partecipazione del sindacato usb è partito da Piazza Arbarello per contribuire a bloccare la città arrivando fino a confindustria. 


Lo spezzone sociale ha visto alternarsi al microfono una miriade di voci differenti capaci di rappresentare l’anima e lo spirito della città che non si arrende e che combatte contro il carovita di guerra. Dalle Valli di Lanzo, dalla Val di Susa, fino a Barriera di Milano ogni presa di parola ha saputo contribuire a costruire la direzione comune della lotta. 


Una volta arrivati in corso Vittorio lo spezzone sociale non ha voluto accontentarsi del misero percorso concordato dalla CGIL ma ha voluto continuare, dribblando sapientemente i blocchi dei reparti celere e dell’idrante, fino a giungere dopo una lunga marcia fino all’imbocco della autostrada sud. Lì un ingente dispiegamento di polizia con l’idrante ha impedito ai manifestanti di salire sulla rampa autostradale, ma ha di fatto bloccato la circolazione regalando un gol di sponda a chi ha marciato per ore per raggiungere corso Trieste a Moncalieri. 


Tornati indietro verso piazza Bengasi, il corteo si è sciolto, ma per riconvocarsi nuovamente alle 18 in piazza Castello, ormai luogo simbolo della mobilitazione contro il carovita e delle lotte cittadine. Dopo un momento festoso, in cui un coro autorganizzato si è esibito in omaggio alla mobilitazione, il corteo è partito più determinato che mai per le vie del centro cittadino, cercando di sbaragliare, e riuscendoci più volte, i reparti celere e dei carabinieri. In via Accademia Albertina la polizia ha dovuto respingere più tentativi di sfondamento da parte del corteo, come in via della Rocca e su corso Cairoli. Il corteo ha proseguito su corso Casale ritornando verso piazza Vittorio e bloccando il traffico serale. Sul ponte della Gran Madre idrante e celerini si sono scontrati con la determinazione del corteo ad oltrepassare nuovamente il P,o dovendo ricorrere all’uso dei lacrimogeni. Con grande entusiasmo e voglia di continuare la lotta, ci si è lasciati in piazza Borromini con la promessa di rincontrarsi il giorno seguente per il compleanno dei 30 anni di Askatasuna in piazza Santa Giulia. 


Da più di un mese un enorme numero di persone sta scendendo in strada a manifestare contro il carovita e il riarmo ogni fine settimana, il 20 novembre è il sesto di fila. Un fatto inedito, e meraviglioso, il 28 sarà il settimo e in pochi hanno voglia di fermarsi!


La piazza è il luogo in cui ci ritroviamo per lottare ma anche per conoscerci e organizzarci. Le scuole e le università occupate ci hanno insegnato come si strappa il potere di mano a chi comanda le nostre vite e come lo si trasforma in qualcosa di diverso e al servizio dei nostri bisogni. 


Noi la guerra non la paghiamo!


Il governo Meloni se ne deve andare, tutti i governi se ne devono andare, il futuro possiamo costruirlo insieme senza di loro.

title: Yeni Parti’li Murat Emir: “İzleme Komisyonu kararı, barış irademizde bir değişiklik anlamına gelmez”
content:
Yeni Parti Grup Başkanvekili Murat Emir, partisinin Meclis bünyesinde kurulması planlanan İzleme Komisyonu'na üye vermeme kararına ilişkin kapsamlı bir açıklama yayımladı. Emir sosyal medya hesabından yayımladığı açıklamada, komisyonda yer almama kararının barış iradesinden vazgeçildiği anlamına gelmeyeceğini vurguladı.

Emir, "Barışa verdiğimiz destek, iktidarın her tercihine peşinen verilmiş onay olarak anlaşılamaz. Demokratikleşmenin ertelenmesine itirazımız da toplumsal barıştan vazgeçtiğimiz anlamına gelmez. Şehit ailelerinin ve gazilerimizin hassasiyetlerini, çatışmalarda evladını kaybetmiş ailelerin acısını, yıllardır adalet bekleyenlerin sesini aynı sorumlulukla dikkate alıyoruz" ifadelerini kullandı. Barışın pazarlık konusu yapılamayacağını ancak demokrasi olmadan da kalıcı barışın kurulamayacağını vurgulayan Emir, iktidarın anayasal yükümlülüklerini sürecin sonuna ertelemesine tepki gösterdi.

Demokratikleşmenin artık ertelenemeyeceğini vurgulayan Emir, “Barış pazarlık konusu yapılamaz ancak, demokrasi olmadan da kalıcı barışın kurulamayacağı unutulmamalıdır. Silahların susmasını hiçbir siyasi pazarlığın şartına bağlamıyoruz. Aynı şekilde, Anayasa’nın uygulanmasının ve yurttaşların haklarına kavuşmasının da bir pazarlığın sonucuna ertelenmesini kabul etmiyoruz” vurgusu yaptı.

Kalıcı barışın demokratik güvencelerini istemenin, silahsızlanmanın önüne yeni bir şart koymak olmadığını belirten Emir, “İktidarın zaten yerine getirmekle yükümlü olduğu sorumluluklar barışın ön şartı olamayacağı gibi, mahkeme kararlarına uymak için veya kayyım uygulamasına artık son vermek için sürecin tamamlanması beklenemez. Basın ve ifade özgürlüğünün önündeki engellerin kaldırılması, iktidarın uygun zaman geldiğinde sunacağı bir imkân olarak görülemez. Biz, toplumsal barış umudunun otoriter uygulamalara gerekçe yapılmasına itiraz ediyoruz. Barışı savunmanın bedeli, hukuksuzluklar karşısında susmak olmamalıdır” ifadelerini kullandı.

Komisyon raporunun 6.5’inci bölümünde yer alan, yürütme içinde bir izleme mekanizması oluşturulması ve hazırlanacak raporların TBMM’ye sunulmasının öngörüldüğünü hatırlatan Emir şu ifadelere yer verdi:

“Bu bölümde, milletvekillerinden oluşacak yeni bir izleme komisyonu kurulması önerisi bulunmamaktadır. Rapordaki ifade açıktır: Yürütme tarafından bu konuda hazırlanacak raporların TBMM’ye sunulması gerekli görülmektedir. 6.1’inci bölümde ise tespit ve teyidin nesnel, ölçülebilir ve denetlenebilir ölçütlerle, şeffaf biçimde yürütülmesi istenmektedir. Sonradan kabul edilen 7595 sayılı Kanun’un 7’nci maddesinin beşinci fıkrasında Meclis bünyesinde İzleme Komisyonu kurulması düzenlenmiştir. Raporun önerileri ile sonradan kanunlaştırılan hükümleri birbirine karıştırmadan konuşmak gerekir.”

Yeni Parti’nin Çerçeve Yasa’ya verdiği desteğin, silahların susması için üstlenilen sorumluluğun gereği olarak tanımlayan Emir, “Bu destek, yasanın uygulanışına ilişkin eleştiri ve denetim hakkımızdan vazgeçtiğimiz anlamına gelmez. Yeni kurulması planlanan İzleme Komisyonu’na ilişkin kararımız da bu siyasi sorumluluk içinde değerlendirilmelidir. Aynı raporun yedinci bölümünde AYM ve AİHM kararlarına uyulması, ifade ve basın özgürlüğünün güçlendirilmesi, infazda adalet, siyasi partilerin kurumsal kimliklerinin korunması ve görevden uzaklaştırılan belediye başkanlarının yerine belediye meclislerinin seçim yapması yönünde öneriler de bulunmaktadır. İktidar temsilcilerinin de kabul ettiği bu öneriler, raporun ayrılmaz parçasıdır. Altıncı bölümü uygularken yedinci bölümü belirsiz bir geleceğe bırakamazsınız. Biz imzamızın sorumluluğunu taşıyoruz. Aynı sorumluluğu, rapora imza atan herkesten bekliyoruz” ifadelerine yer verdi.

YENİ Parti’nin İzleme Komisyonu’na üye vermeme kararı, barış irademizde bir değişiklik anlamına gelmemektedir. Silahların susması, şiddetin sona ermesi ve Türkiye’nin bütün yurttaşları için huzurlu bir geleceğin kurulması için bugüne kadar sorumluluk aldık; aynı sorumlulukla hareket etmeyi sürdürüyoruz. author: Rizomatica
title: 159 años de la creación del fuerte militar de Collipulli y una violencia simbólica que nadie quiere ver pero que todos ven
content:
Por estos días de noviembre se conmemora el aniversario de la comuna y pueblo de Collipulli. Precisamente el 22 de noviembre de 1867. Fue en el contexto de la Ocupación Militar de la Araucanía por parte del estado Chileno quien decide invadir Wallmapu o territorio Mapuche, rompiendo y desconociendo el tratado de Tapihue de 1825 el cual en 1861 aprueba el plan de ocupación militar para la Araucanía al mando de Cornelio Saavedra. Este plan contenía en una primera fase la ocupación de la frontera entre los ríos Bio- Bio y Malleco. Fue entonces que a partir de 1867 empieza una segunda fase de esta ocupación militar la cual consistía en una línea de fuertes sobre el río Malleco desde la cordillera de Nahuelbuta hasta la cordillera de los Andes. Es ahí que funda los fuertes de Curaco, Perasco, COLLIPULLI, Mariluan, Chiwaiwe ,Lolenco, Cancura y Huequen .


La fortificación en una línea militar del río Malleco tenía como lógica el avance y posterior ocupación del territorio sobre las fuerzas Mapuche que se opusieron tenazmente a la invasión militar del ejército chileno, estamos hablando de la identidad territorial Huenteche, en las tierras del lonko Kilapan- hijo del gran lonko Mañil Huenu- además de Huentecol, Kilahueque, entre otros. Dichos territorios se conocen en la actualidad como «la Zona Roja». Sectores como Bajo Malleco, Pidima, Ercilla, Temucuicui, Chamichaco, Pailahueque, Victoria, Perquenco, Lautaro y otros, han sido epicentros del conflicto entre el estado Chileno y el pueblo Mapuche. Pues bien,  en el tiempo de la ocupación  militar del siglo XIX  y la fundación del fuerte Collipulli, se conoció como la «Guarida de los facinerosos» este último concepto, según el libro La Historia del Despojo, del historiador Martin Correa Cabrera.


Con la fundación de dichos fuertes, la guerra avanza en forma encarnizada  en detrimento del pueblo Mapuche y el río Malleco se transformó en una carnicería.  Las fuerzas Mapuche combatieron hasta lo que más pudieron en esta guerra desigual y cobarde por parte del estado Chileno. El uso del fusil de repetición inclina la balanza en favor de las tropas chilenas y finalmente en 1881, las fuerzas Mapuche son derrotadas en el llamado Futamalon de 1881 y en 1883 el ejército Chileno llega a Villarrica dando por terminada la ocupación militar de la Araucanía; Ocupación que trajo como consecuencia la perdida del 95% de nuestro territorio, es decir, de 10 millones de hectáreas  quedamos reducidos a 500 mil; el genocidio y casi la desaparición de nuestro pueblo a consecuencia de esta guerra, además de haber roto el tejido social y político, por ende de nuestra soberania cómo pueblo.


CONCEPTO DE VIOLENCIA SIMBÓLICA Y SU MANIFESTACIÓN EN COLLIPULLI 


Hay que decir que el concepto de violencia simbólica fue utilizado por el sociólogo Pierre Burdieu refiriéndose a la escuela y al sistema educativo. Este concepto se refiere a un tipo de violencia que no usa la fuerza física, si no que es a través de los símbolos, lenguaje, discursos, manifestaciones culturales entre muchas otras destinado a crear una relación desigual de poder entre diversos grupos de una sociedad. Creando una categorización entre  grupos dominados y grupos dominadores. Son precisamente los símbolos, lenguaje, signos culturales y discursos de este último grupo,los que predominan en una sociedad cuando se da este tipo de violencia simbólica. En tanto los grupos dominados asumen como normal y legítimo este tipo de conducta porque forma parte de una conducta reiterada que está presente en la sociedad desde mucho antes que ellos nacieran, por lo tanto la normalizan, legitiman y también la defienden.


Con este antecedente es importante decir que Collipulli es un pueblo muy especial. 


La plaza de armas de Collipulli lleva por nombre: Plaza» Diego Barros Arana» , historiador Chileno del siglo XIX mismo que a mediados y fines de ese siglo argumentaba que el problema de la Araucanía es que había

  «indios malos en tierras buenas» 

.


Dicha plaza en el medio contiene un monumento al encargado de la ocupación militar de la Araucanía, Cornelio Saavedra, principal genocida estratégico del pueblo Mapuche. Al costado de dicho busto de Saavedra se encuentran dos Cañones de la ocupación militar, los cuales fueron encontrados cerca de 1950 en las inmediaciones de uno de los fuertes en la del río Malleco, lugar donde se dió la guerra encarnizada en contra del pueblo Mapuche. author: webadmin
title: Where Is The Hunting Ban, Labour?
content:
This fox was illegally hunted at a joint meet of the North Cotswold Hunt and the Warwickshire Hunt on Saturday 14th November. Image credit: West Midlands Hunt Sabs


In July 2024, the Labour Government made a manifesto commitment to ban trail hunting and improve the Hunting Act.


On 26 March 2026, the Government launched a consultation to determine how best to implement an effective and enforceable ban on trail hunting in England and Wales.


The consultation closed on 18 June, having received 184,000 responses. Yet months later, we are still waiting for the results and a clear timetable for what happens next.


The Government has acknowledged the risks trail hunting poses to wildlife, including the danger of hounds pursuing and killing live animals. It has also recognised concerns that trail hunting can be used as a smokescreen for illegal hunting.


This fox was hunted and killed by the Blackmore and Sparkford Vale (BSV) Hunt on Thursday 19th November. Image credit: Locals Against The BSV Hunt


Meanwhile, wildlife continues to suffer.


Foxes and other wild animals are chased, injured and killed. Our local hunt saboteur groups are out week after week, witnessing and documenting incidents and working to protect wildlife, often with little support.


But hunting also affects people. Rural residents face disruption, trespass, intimidation, road safety issues and damage to property. Their experiences should not be overlooked.


The Countryside Alliance and British Hound Sports Association continue to portray a ban on trail hunting as an attack on rural communities, livelihoods and countryside traditions.


But protecting wildlife and rural communities is not an attack on the countryside. Nor should legitimate countryside activities be used as a justification for allowing hunting with dogs to continue.


A ban must be comprehensive. Simply banning trail hunting is not enough if exemptions and loopholes allow hunts to continue pursuing and killing wildlife under another guise.


The HSA is calling for a full and effective ban on hunting with dogs, removing the existing exemptions and loopholes that allow this cruelty to continue, alongside meaningful improvements to the Hunting Act.


WE NEED THE GOVERNMENT TO ACT


We are demanding three things:


Publish the consultation results and the Government’s response.


Publish the legislative proposals for a full and effective ban on hunting with dogs and improvements to the Hunting Act, removing exemptions and loopholes.


Set a clear date for introducing the necessary legislation to Parliament.


We cannot allow this commitment to disappear into the political long grass.


Wildlife needs protection now, not at some unspecified point in the future.


TAKE ACTION


PLEASE TAKE ACTION TODAY


We need as many people as possible to contact their elected representatives and make it clear that this issue has not gone away.


Write to your MP


Ask your MP to contact the Government and demand answers to the three questions above. Ask them to press for a clear timetable and support a comprehensive ban on hunting with dogs, without exemptions or loopholes. Write to your MP

here

.


Write to the Prime Minister


The Prime Minister has spoken about building a more caring society. That must include compassion and protection for our wildlife.


Ask him to ensure the Government honours its commitment to ban trail hunting and delivers the wider legislative changes needed to end hunting with dogs. Write to the Prime Minister

here

.


Both messages can be brief. What matters is that MPs and the Prime Minister hear from as many people as possible.


Our wildlife cannot wait any longer. We need a full ban, effective legislation and an end to the loopholes that allow this cruelty to continue.


NOW IS THE TIME TO MAKE OUR VOICES HEARD.


TAKE ACTION
